#2646. MLB qualifying offer: Predicting who will get a QO this offseason, plus how the $23.15 million contract works

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Brewers have been crowned the 2026 World Series champions and the 2026-27 offseason is already underway. More than 100 players became free agents the day after the World Series ended, and soon teams will have to make decisions about contract options and qualifying offers.

The qualifying offer (QO) entitles teams to draft-pick compensation in the event that they lose a free agent to another team. The QO is a one-year deal set at the average of the top 125 salaries in baseball. This offseason, it's worth a record $23.15 million, according to the New York Post. That is up from $22.025 million last year, $21.05 million the year before, and $20.325 million the year before that.

Teams have until five days after the end of the World Series to tender their free agents the QO, and players who receive it then have until 4 p.m. ET on Nov. 17 to accept or reject. Players who accept the QO remain with their team and cannot be traded without their consent until June 15. Players who reject the QO become free agents with draft-pick compensation attached.

Simple, right? The process is, but the decisions aren't always. With that in mind, let's run down this offseason's QO candidates, as well as explain the draft-pick compensation rules.

Yes, the QO is still a thing this offseason. The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and the next CBA could change the QO rules, maybe even eliminate it entirely. That said, until that happens, the QO remains in place. Decisions to tender the QO (made by the team) and decisions to accept or reject the QO (made by the player) are due before the CBA expires.

Once upon a time, teams that lost an eligible free agent received a compensation draft pick after the first round. It was nice and easy. The current rules are a bit more complicated. Here are compensation rules for teams that lose a qualified free agent:

Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round)

Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round)

The Athletics, Brewers, Cardinals, Diamondbacks, Guardians, Mariners, Marlins, Orioles, Pirates, Rays, Reds, Rockies, Royals, Tigers, and Twins received revenue sharing this season, so the first two scenarios apply to them. The Blue Jays, Braves, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, Red Sox, and Yankees will pay competitive balance tax (CBT), so they're in the third scenario. The Angels, Astros, Giants, Nationals, Rangers, and White Sox neither received revenue sharing nor paid CBT. They're in the fourth bucket.

Now here are the penalties for signing a qualified free agent:

The Blue Jays, Braves, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, Red Sox, and Yankees will pay CBT and are in the first group. The Athletics, Brewers, Cardinals, Diamondbacks, Guardians, Mariners, Marlins, Orioles, Pirates, Rays, Reds, Rockies, Royals, Tigers, and Twins received revenue sharing and are in the second group. The Angels, Astros, Giants, Nationals, Rangers, and White Sox are the third group. Got it? Good.

Thirteen players received the QO last offseason: Trent Grisham, Shota Imanaga, Gleyber Torres, and Brandon Woodruff accepted the QO; Zac Gallen, Michael King, and Kyle Schwarber declined but signed new contracts to remain with their teams; Bo Bichette, Dylan Cease, Edwin Díaz, Kyle Tucker, Ranger Suárez, and Framber Valdez rejected the QO and signed with new teams, giving their former clubs compensatory draft picks. Teams do not gain or lose draft picks for re-signing their own qualified free agent.

Players are eligible for the QO as long as they spent the entire 2026 season with one team and did not receive the QO previously. That means several high-profile free agents are not eligible for the QO this offseason. Here are the notables:

CHANGED TEAMS Luis Arraez Kevin Gausman (also received QO previously) Casey Mize Freddy Peralta Tarik Skubal Daulton Varsho

PREVIOUSLY RECEIVED QO Bo Bichette (opt out) Sonny Gray (mutual option) Michael King (opt out)  Nick Martinez

The Tigers traded Skubal, the reigning two-time AL Cy Young winner, to the Dodgers for a three-prospect package at the deadline. MLB Pipeline currently ranks those players as Detroit's No. 1 (Zyhir Hope), No. 3 (River Ryan), and No. 9 (Brady Smith) prospects. That's a much better haul than the compensation draft pick the Tigers would have received had they kept Skubal all year and made him the QO. Anyway, these free agents are among those not eligible for the QO this offseason.

This is not the best free agent class and, as a result, I count only two stone-cold locks to receive a QO: Randy Arozarena (Mariners) and Seiya Suzuki (Cubs). The Mariners and Cubs would be thrilled if Arozarena and Seiya accepted the QO and returned next season on one-year contracts that aren't too much of a raise. Arozarena made $15.65 million this year. Suzuki earned $18 million. The jump to $23.15 million isn't big enough to shy away from the QO, plus these are really good players. Arozarena and Suzuki will receive the QO and decline it.

Although Arozarena and Suzuki are the only locks to get the QO, in my opinion, there are three other free agents-to-be who seem like pretty good bets to receive it. Here are those three players:

Ryan Jeffers, Twins: Jeffers will be the best catcher to hit the open market since Willson Contreras four years ago. He missed time with a hamate injury this year and his defense isn't great, plus he'll turn 30 next June. Those seem like nitpicks compared to the offense he brings to the table at the catcher position. The only reason I don't think Jeffers is a lock to get the QO is the fact that the Twins have shaved roughly $50 million off their payroll the last four years. They might get thrifty.

Brandon Lowe, Pirates: Pittsburgh knocked it out of the park with the Mike Burrows-for-Lowe-and-Mason Montgomery three-team trade with the Astros and Rays. Montgomery is a bullpen ace and Lowe slugged 35 home runs, the most by a Pirate since Josh Bell hit 37 in 2019. Lowe's age (32), poor contact rates, and history of poor defense (though not in 2026) create collapse risk. Also, the Pirates run a bottom 10 payroll every season. I expect Lowe to get the QO. I just wouldn't be surprised if the Pirates decide not to risk him taking it, thereby soaking up 20% or so of their 2027 payroll.

Trevor Rogers, Orioles: Rogers, 29 in November, was a bright spot in an otherwise lost season for the O's. He stayed healthy and threw a career-high 169 ⅔ innings, and pitched exceptionally well after June 1: 2.90 ERA with under-the-hood numbers to match (2.89 FIP and 3.10 expected ERA). Rogers might be the second-best free agent starter behind Skubal given his success the last two years and (more importantly) analytically friendly arsenal. During the president of baseball operations Mike Elias era, the Orioles haven't always done the most sensible thing when it comes to spending money. I think it's 99% certain the O's will give Rogers the QO, but 99% is not 100%.

My hunch is teams will be conservative with their QO decisions this offseason because a new CBA is coming, and no one knows what the game's economic landscape will look like next year. Will there be a salary cap? More punitive CBT penalties? I would expect teams to err on the side of caution when it comes to potentially committing $23.15 million to one player. Even a good player they may want back, but not necessarily at $23.15 million in 2027. Here are three borderline QO cases:

David Bednar, Yankees: Bednar has proven he can close games in New York, which is not nothing, but he did just turn 32, and the $23.15 million QO would make him the highest-paid reliever in baseball. I think the Yankees want to bring Bednar back next season. Enough to risk him accepting the QO? When the potential reward is a dinky draft pick after the fourth round given their CBT status? That I'm not sold on. A multi-year contract at a lower annual salary is the much more likely path to Bednar returning to the Yankees.

Jazz Chisholm Jr., Yankees: Even in a down year, Chisholm was a 3.5-WAR player thanks to the breadth of his skill set. He hit 19 homers, he stole 41 bases, and he was fourth among second basemen with +13 outs above average. The all-around game and the fact that Chisholm will play the entire 2027 season at age 29 would seem to make him a slam dunk QO candidate. My sense is the Yankees won't commit any significant payroll to next season without first seeing what the new CBA brings, which is exactly what they did before the last lockout. I think the Yankees value the payroll flexibility (i.e. the certainty that Chisholm won't take the QO) more than the post-fourth round compensation pick they would receive if he signed elsewhere.

Adrian Morejon, Padres: Morejon will be an interesting test case for San Diego's new ownership. He is outstanding, one of the five or six best relievers in baseball, and he'll play the entire 2027 season at age 28. The QO would make Morejon the highest-paid reliever in the game, but only if he takes it, and his age and effectiveness would seem to make that unlikely. Do the Padres roll the dice and give Morejon the QO, and risk sinking $23.15 million into a (great) setup man, or not bother because they're only in line to receive a draft pick after the fourth round if he leaves? Díaz, Josh Hader (from the Padres), and Raisel Iglesias are the only relievers to get the QO in the last seven years. Is Morejon in that class?

#2645. Tyrese Haliburton becomes latest injured NBA star: Pacers guard 'week-to-week' with hamstring strain

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tyrese Haliburton's return to the Pacers lineup after missing the entire 2025-26 season with an Achilles tear has hit a speed bump, as the All-Star guard deals with a hamstring strain four games into the year.

Pacers coach Rick Carlisle said Wednesday that after meeting with doctors, Haliburton would be considered "week-to-week" with his hamstring strain and is unlikely to play in the next two weeks.

"It's not good news, but it could be worse," Carlisle told reporters (via the Indianapolis Star).

Haliburton, who sat out all of last season after suffering a torn Achilles in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals, has been terrific for the Pacers in his return to the court, averaging 21.8 points, 9.5 assists and 4.5 rebounds per game on 51.6/37.0/86.7 shooting splits over Indiana's first four games. After hitting some clutch shots in the opener, Haliburton was overcome with emotion thinking about his journey back to the basketball court, and now he will have to find that patience once again as he waits for his hamstring to heal enough to play again.

The Pacers will be without Haliburton for a big game on Wednesday night against the 76ers, with games against the Heat, Nets and Hawks up on the schedule over the next week.

Indiana will try to navigate that stretch not only without their star guard, but with Ivica Zubac and TJ McConnell as players also listed as out on Wednesday's injury report, while Andrew Nembhard is questionable with a neck/back injury.

That's a considerable amount of Indiana's guard depth that either can't play or will be playing at less than 100 percent, along with their top center. That shifts Pascal Siakam back into a lead role offensively and forces the Pacers into more small-ball lineups with Obi Toppin at the five.

For a team trying to get back into the conversation in the Eastern Conference after a lost season in 2025-26, seeing injuries pile up early in the year is extremely frustrating and disheartening. The Pacers were a half of basketball away from winning a championship when Haliburton tore his Achilles in Game 7 against the Thunder and have spent more than a year waiting to get him back to try to make the climb again.

While Carlisle noted in a radio interview on Wednesday morning the hope was Haliburton's hamstring wouldn't be a long-term injury, soft tissue injuries always bring some concern. The Pacers will have to balance patience with the desire to not fall too far behind in a suddenly stacked East.

Haliburton's injury continues a frustrating trend in the early NBA season, which has seen a tremendous number of top players listed on injury reports. The list of stars currently on the shelf with injuries is staggering, with the likes of Anthony Edwards, Jalen Williams, Paolo Banchero, Kawhi Leonard, Jaren Jackson Jr., Chet Holmgren and Alperen Sengun all currently listed out for games on Wednesday night. That's not to mention players like Brandon Ingram, Jimmy Butler, Kon Knueppel and Kristaps Porzingis who have yet to make their season debuts.

While it feels like an absurd number of injuries this early in the season, it's much closer to par for the course than the NBA would probably like to admit. Stars being injured has become a constant concern in recent years, but there isn't an obvious solution.

The NBA schedule is often discussed as a reason for the volume of injuries, but this early in the season, it's hard to point to the wear-and-tear of an 82-game grind. Instead, it feels more like a byproduct of a style of play that pushes players to their limits. The speed of the game is tremendous now and players are pushing their bodies to play faster and more explosively, which raises the potential for injuries.

That's an even harder thing to solve than schedule reform -- which the league and players aren't particularly interested in -- because playing with pace and maximizing possessions is proven to be the most effective style in the modern era.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only two days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

As expected, Mets infielder Bo Bichette has picked up his $42 million player option for 2027, reports The Athletic. He holds another $42 million player option for 2028. Still only 28, Bichette had a poor first season in Queens, posting a .702 OPS with 18 home runs while showing growing pains as he transitioned from shortstop over to third base.

For now, the Mets are set on the infield with Bichette at third, Francisco Lindor at short, and Marcus Semien at second. They must figure out first base, and it is possible they will make a trade to shake up that veteran infield. Moving Semien would be ideal, but it may not be doable. Lindor's name figures to pop up in trade rumors against this offseason.

The Diamondbacks are expected to listen to offers for second baseman Ketel Marte, reports the Arizona Republic. The D-backs entertained trade offers last offseason, but were unable to find a match. Marte has full no-trade protection and can direct where he lands, if he wants to leave Arizona at all. His desire to change teams is unknown.

Marte, 33, had a down year by his standards in 2026. He also went AWOL in August, prompting the D-backs to put him on the restricted list. Manager Torey Lovullo later revealed it was the fourth straight season Marte missed a game without permission. Beyond the on-field fit, teams will have to weigh the potential clubhouse impact and headaches.

The Seibu Lions in Japan will make right-hander Kaima Taira available to MLB teams via the posting system this offseason, the team announced Friday. The posting is expected to be made official in the coming days. Once that happens, Taira will have 45 days to negotiate and sign with an MLB team, otherwise he will return to Japan in 2027.

We ranked Taira as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason. Here's our write-up:

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man.

Taira, 27 next month, threw 146 innings with a 1.36 ERA and 141 strikeouts this past season. He actually had higher ERAs as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, though he has been excellent throughout his career in Japan, and has the bat-missing power stuff that tends to translate well to MLB. Taira figures to be highly sought after in the coming weeks.

The trading season resumed Thursday and the Red Sox were involved in the offseason's first two trades. First, they sent utility man Nate Eaton to the Athletics for minor-league righty Jareth Rayo, the team announced. The A's recently named former Red Sox assistant general manager Taylor Smith their new president of baseball operations. His first move was bringing in Eaton, a player he's presumably familiar with given their overlapping time in Boston.

Next, the Red Sox traded infielder Tsung-Che Cheng to the Tigers for cash, the team announced. Cheng, 25, is a glove-first utility man who appeared in 14 games with Boston this past season. Both the Cheng and Eaton trades open up 40-man roster spots for the Red Sox, who still must open three more spots to accommodate their seven players on the 60-day injured list. They must be activated no later than this coming Monday.

#2640. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2639. Astros hire Randy Flores as new general manager as offseason filled with questions begins in Houston

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros' search for a new head of baseball operations has ended with the hiring of Randy Flores as general manager. The 51-year-old Flores had been an assistant general manager with the St. Louis Cardinals. In Houston, Flores replaces Dana Brown, who was let go in late August. Flores becomes the fourth head of baseball operations to serve under Astros owner Jim Crane.

"Randy has had a huge impact on the Cardinals over the last 10 seasons," Crane said in a statement released by the club. "Throughout the entire interview process, we've been thoroughly impressed with Randy and his background in scouting and player acquisition. We're happy to welcome Randy and his family to the Astros and we can't wait to get to work on bringing another championship to Houston."

Added Flores: "I am excited and grateful for this amazing opportunity. The Astros have a long winning tradition under Jim Crane, and I look forward to contributing to the success.  I want to thank the Cardinals organization for the opportunities and support that made this next chapter possible. My family and I are excited to make Houston home."

Flores for roughly a decade served as scouting director for the Cardinals and was tasked with running their draft. He added the assistant GM title in 2018 and saw his portfolio of responsibilities expand within the last year.

Flores takes over an Astros organization beset by uncertainty. With an aging roster and after several key departures over the years, the Astros have seen their season-long win total decline for four straight years. This past season, the Astros eked out the American League Central title but finished with a .500 record and a negative run differential. In terms of success and roster strength, they're a long way from their dynasty years of 2017-22. It's not certain whether the Astros moving forward will try to squeeze out another season of relevance or embrace a rebuild, but either path will have its challenges.

Speaking of challenges, Crane and his trusted advisor Jeff Bagwell have been an increasingly meddlesome presence in recent years, and it's unclear to what degree Flores will have autonomy in his role. Whatever the future holds, Flores' first major decision is filling the managerial vacancy. After the end of the regular season, Crane opted not to renew the contract of former manager Joe Espada.

Prior to beginning his front office career, Flores spent parts of eight seasons in the majors as a left-handed reliever. In 2006, he earned a World Series ring as a member of that Cardinals team.

#2636. Five ways the NBA's injury outbreak could impact trade season: OKC has work to do, Rockets are in control

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

At a bare minimum we're still six weeks away from the unofficial start of NBA trade season. It's still October, and a bit less than one-third of the league is still not trade-eligible because they signed new contracts in free agency. The moves usually don't begin until Dec. 15, when the bulk of those players become trade-eligible.

The strategizing for those moves, however, is a never-ending process, and even though we've only seen nine days worth of games, the entire league landscape has already been turned on its head by one of the earliest injury outbreaks in NBA history. Let's do a quick roll call: Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace, Jaren Jackson Jr., Tyrese Haliburton, Kawhi Leonard, Anthony Edwards and Paolo Banchero are all out with injuries that should sideline them for weeks or months at best and all season at worst. Their teams suddenly have to figure out how to manage without their best players... but everyone else has to figure out what those absences mean in the long run.

Again... we're barely a week into the season. The market could change drastically again in eight days or eight weeks. We're more than three months away from the deadline. But so much has already happened that it's worth taking a step back and figuring out what this could mean when the deals eventually start coming. Here are five ripple effects the early rash of injuries could have on the trade market.

Think about the trades Oklahoma City tends to make. They're almost always from a position of strength. They traded Paul George to the Clippers when they had them at their mercy during Kawhi Leonard's free agency. They didn't proactively seek out Alex Caruso. They were looking to move Josh Giddey when the perfect role player fell into their laps. They got Jared McCain with a spare first-round pick because Daryl Morey thought he was selling high. The only notable, recent occasion in which the Thunder have added a notable veteran based on an immediate need was Isaiah Hartenstein, who came in free agency. The Thunder typically don't have needs. They develop players to address them before they arise.

Well, because of injuries, the Thunder suddenly do have needs. The bare minimum here is a versatile, forward-sized defender. They tried to steal Spencer Jones from the Nuggets over the summer for this exact purpose. At the time, they likely viewed Jones or Jones-esque defender as a luxury. Now, someone like that is a necessity. Oklahoma City's formerly endless rotation of All-Defense-caliber point-of-attack stoppers is now down to Caruso, who's already sporting an ankle sprain. Their playing style is enormously reliant on this archetype for turnover generation and transition offense.

There are half-court offensive questions as well. We all saw what Victor Wembanyama did to Shai Gilgeous-Alexander without Williams in the Western Conference Finals. Ajay Mitchell is healthy now. He wasn't in that series. How his next few months play out will tell the Thunder whether or not they have to upgrade the offense as well. They can't expect to score on Wembanyama if their offense devolves into nothing but Gilgeous-Alexander mid-range jumpers. Eventually, Alex Caruso is going to miss a playoff 3-pointer.

So for the first time since perhaps the Kevin Durant era, the Thunder, and their endless reserves of assets, go into a trade deadline with obvious needs and an imperative to address them. This roster gets more expensive by the year. The Thunder can't afford to waste a season. Their financial limitations are significant, but Sam Presti is the NBA's best general manager. If there is a way to keep the Thunder up to speed with Wembanyama and the Spurs, he's going to find it.

Oklahoma City's vulnerability trickles down to everyone else. We entered the season assuming a Thunder-Spurs conference finals rematch was inevitable. The Thunder are weakened. The entire rest of the West is one Wembanyama ankle sprain away from 2027 becoming their best chance for the foreseeable future. The Lakers, the Nuggets and the Timberwolves suddenly have far more reason to be aggressive than they did 10 days ago. The problem is that all three of them are working with limited means of improvement:

Minnesota is obviously dealing with the trickiest situation of the three since Edwards is already hurt. They can't justify a win-now move until they have a better sense of how healthy he'll be in the spring. And yet, with Rudy Gobert in his age-34 season and the Thunder more beatable than ever, they might have to roll those dice. Can they really justify holding onto Donte DiVincenzo's contract considering he might not return from his torn Achilles this season, for example? He's someone they hope to keep as a long-term bench fixture. He's also the only notable salary Minnesota can use to add someone who can help now, when the West seems winnable.

The Lakers are starting two minimum-salary wings, and their backup center minutes have been atrocious. The Nuggets are winless against teams besides the Pelicans. These are talented yet flawed teams staring down a future in a conference that features two younger, deeper and better juggernauts. This is an opportunity that may not repeat itself. The ones who take it will be in far better shape than the ones who don't.

The Rockets have the same newfound sense of urgency that the Lakers, Nuggets and Wolves do... under a completely different set of internal circumstances. They have a sizable draft pick surplus. They have salaries of every size to trade. They're also undefeated, including a win over San Antonio that underlined their meaningful advantages in that matchup Alperen Sengun is one of the few bigs in the NBA that tends to enjoy attacking Wembanyama. They have the perimeter defensive depth to handle San Antonio's guards. The Rockets, of those four non-Thunder or Spurs West contenders, probably should feel the best about their ability to win the title right now, with what they already have.

That puts the Rockets where the Thunder usually sit: a position of strength. There's an obvious need to fill when it comes to adding another shot-creator, but their ability to trade for basically anyone across the salary or asset spectrum with the leverage to tell any trade partner "no thanks, we're good enough as is" gives them control of the board. They can outbid just about any rival suitor for just about any theoretically available player if they so choose, effectively giving them right of first refusal over most of the trade landscape unless the Thunder or Spurs are prepared to take on contracts bigger than we'd presently expect.

So much of what's happening in the West starts with Oklahoma City. Those same ripples aren't felt in the East. There, teams are much more concerned with themselves than their competitors.

Take the Raptors. They have RJ Barrett on an expiring contract and a clear need for more shooting. With a healthy Kawhi Leonard, Barrett's individual creation might be a luxury. With him injured, it's a necessity. The Thunder can't really evaluate Barrett's fit on the Leonard-centric version of their team until Leonard returns, and they can't consider whether or not there's a way to flip Barrett into more shooting until they know how important he is to their actual roster.

The Pacers are adapting to playing with a center that cannot shoot 3s. That's a fairly traditional basketball problem, but it's still new to a team that reached the Finals on the strength of its shooting. The Haliburton-Ivica Zubac tandem has only played 52 minutes together thus far, and with Haliburton sidelined, it'll be awhile until Indiana gets a bigger sample than that. Those two are going to be fixtures for the Pacers, but Indiana is still relatively liquid from a draft pick perspective and has serious questions to address on the bench. A clearer idea of where that duo is deficient, if anywhere, would help the Pacers figure out what sort of bench help to target.

And then there's Orlando. Poor, poor Orlando. For the third straight season, Paolo Banchero has suffered a meaningful injury in October or November. In each of the last two seasons, Franz Wagner took on a bigger role while Banchero was out and eventually got hurt himself right around Banchero's return. The Magic are running out of bullets to fire. They've traded most of their picks for Desmond Bane and they've changed coaches by hiring Sean Sweeney. They're headed for a financial crisis with Anthony Black hitting restricted free agency next summer and their total payroll getting dangerously close to the second apron.

The West trade market changed drastically by virtue of what happened to the Thunder. The opposite is true for the East. These teams haven't gotten new information. They're awaiting information they assumed they'd be getting in the early weeks of the season but will instead come further down the line. If the rumors start coming in earlier than expected, you should therefore assume that the West is the conference driving most of that activity.

So we've identified why the West contenders are going to be eager to improve. The East isn't there yet, but give it time. In a conference with no clear favorite, there are usually plenty of teams looking for reinforcements. Here's the problem: we don't know where they're going to get them. The NBA has never had fewer obvious sellers than it does right now.

We're in a post-lottery reform world now. Nobody wants to lose. That's not just true in a single-year setting. There are going to be fewer and fewer teams that proactively initiate multi-year teardowns now that there are slightly more plausible paths to building from the middle. Contenders get stripped for parts every offseason because of the aprons. Teams that might have rebuilt in the past are instead going to attempt to be opportunistic about adding players whose teams can no longer afford them.

Now you throw in all of these injuries. Not only does that create an excess of potential buyers, but it also freezes the potential sellers market because there are inevitably going to be teams that outperform their on-paper talent because the schedule just got a bit easier and teams that should be above them in the standings instead fall short because of absences.

There are only four teams we can confidently call sellers right now: the Kings, Pelicans, Nets and Bucks. If you want an idea of how confident these sellers are in their ability to extract value for their veterans, look at Shamit Dua's reporting on the Pelicans. New Orleans still reportedly wants two first-round picks worth of value for Herb Jones... who is averaging less than 18 minutes per game to start the season.

New Orleans has been notoriously averse to trading its players away under Joe Dumars, but remember, the Nets functioned as buyers this offseason when they added Julius Randle. They have historically held their veterans until they've been offered a premium, most notably Kevin Durant, Mikal Bridges and Cam Johnson. That's something to keep in mind as they consider Michael Porter Jr. offers. The Bucks and Kings are so early into rebuilds that their plans, for now, are a bit of a mystery.

All of this together suggests that the teams that are willing to trade veterans expect to get significant returns for them. There are simply more teams that want to add right now than there are teams that want to subtract. We'll get closer to equilibrium in January and February, but for all of the reasons we've outlined, we'll probably be further from it as a whole than we've been at any point over the last several years at least.

#2634. Jaylen Brown insists he never demanded Celtics trade, pushes back on 'false allegations' from Brian Scalabrine

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The messiest drama in the NBA resides in the Northeast corridor, where new Philadelphia 76ers star Jaylen Brown has yet to reach the stage where bygones can be bygones with his old team, the Boston Celtics.

Brown was floated in trade rumors early in the offseason as the Milwaukee Bucks were trying to trade Giannis Antetokounmpo before ultimately getting dealt to Philly in a stunning in-division deal for Paul George. His old running mate, Jayson Tatum, said he was shocked by the move, which Brown finds hard to believe.

Tatum tried to bury any notion of beef between he and Brown, insisting "this ain't f--kin Shaq and Kobe," but Brown is less eager to move on and said it might not be beef but could be "lamb chops and gravy" between the two former teammates.

Amid all of that, former Celtics player and current Celtics TV analyst Brian Scalabrine tried defending Tatum by claiming on his radio show that Brown asked for a trade and actually gave Boston a list of demands this offseason and wanted to be traded if they weren't met.

Brown's reps called that "10,000% a lie" and Brown was asked about it after the Sixers' win on Wednesday night and elaborated further, via the Philly Voice.

"Yeah, I mean, I guess it is what it is. I saw that. I saw Scal, he made some comments. Never had any issues with Scal. I love Scal, but I guess he's doing what he has to do," Brown said. "I can understand why he feels the need to do that, but I have no interest [in] letting any false allegations [follow] me to my next chapter here in Philadelphia. Never. I never demanded a trade. Never made a list of ultimatums. None of the sort. None of that is true, but as of now, I'm going to just stay focused on what's in front of me here in Philadelphia. I've got a tremendous opportunity, and I'm looking forward to that. So, I'm going to just leave the questions for another time, but during the season, I'm going to just focus on what's in front of me."

This seems to put this weeklong saga to rest for now, but with the Celtics visiting Philadelphia in less than two weeks on Nov. 10, it won't be long before the questions pick up again about what exactly happened that led to Brown's departure.

The reason the questions persist is the Celtics' process for trading Brown felt sloppier and more hurried compared to the more surgical, calculated approach that's been the hallmark of Brad Stevens' tenure in charge in Boston. Brown's name surfaced in the Antetokounmpo talks and then never went away, with reports emerging that Boston was shopping him around the league to anyone who would listen.

Doing that after Brown put together an All-NBA campaign in 2025-26 raised eyebrows, and there has been an assumption around the league that something happened behind the scenes to sour the team-player relationship to the point of no return.

Brown indicates he'll address that at an appropriate time but not during the season. Until then, the speculation will continue about what went down in Boston.

#2632. Talking to Icarus Football, the kit designers adding beauty to the game

“Football shirts give off a lot of signals,” Robby Smukler says. “They can indicate what you’re passionate about, where you’re from, and even your politics in some cases. That’s part of what makes them so special as a piece of clothing—there’s really so much that’s tied into a football shirt.”

It’s easy to agree with that sentiment. Combining place, philosophy, art, design, and, for some, religion and a sense of belonging, football shirts are the acceptable fashion piece that allow anyone to make a splash and stand out from the crowd. Whether worn at a match, at a festival, or for a quick trip to the coffee house, jerseys are the accessible statement piece anyone can pull off (or on) with ease.

You might also say that they’re a great way of telling your nosey Red neighbour that you’re a die-hard Blue in that silent “fuck you” kind of way.

Robby is the founder of Icarus Football, a custom kit design service making tailor-made shirts for everyone, from five-a-side teams to semi-pro outfits. Quintessentially one-of-a-kind, their jerseys offer one-off pieces that faithfully highlight the sui generis of each club.

Robby’s dream of being a creative started many years ago when he became fascinated with sketching football-themed creations at an early age. As a child growing up in Philadelphia, he would read up on cities and countries near and far before making jersey and crest designs to pass the time.

From the get-go, imagination and flair were key parts of his approach, and that has continued to this day, allowing him to realize all sorts of concepts for teams from a myriad of backgrounds. “We design shirts with fans of a club in mind rather than players. And fans are increasingly looking for creative designs to wear, whether that be for pick-up games in the park or music festivals.

“I think part of the appeal comes from the colours and designs used on football kits. They’re often a lot more creative and out-there than traditional men’s clothing, so football shirts offer something different. They’re also comfortable, so they fit in with the growing trend towards athleisure,” Robby explains.

Indeed, football jerseys are very in today; whether it’s the new releases by the top clubs or the retro classic continually making a comeback, there is a lot of demand for eye-catching sportswear.

Icarus Football’s jerseys appeal to a wide audience because they are steeped in personality, unique designs, and more. As Robby explains, the shirts they make are inspired by each club’s “history, iconography, imagery, fan culture, location”, offering an antidote to the bland factory-manufactured shirts that clubs and fans are often forced to buy.

Robby and his team offer distinctive, eye-catching shirts that clubs can wear with pride when they take to the field. Fans, too, can appreciate the carnival of colour that defines many of their creations, the tailored detail of the pieces, and the thoughtful artistry, too.

“For us, a design that references a team’s culture and history makes a shirt special. But for it to be totally iconic–it needs to be worn in an interesting context.

“The Holland ’88 and Germany ’90 jerseys are two of the most iconic designs of all time, and deservedly so. They’re amazing designs. But if they weren’t worn by those trophy-winning teams and wrapped up in those historic moments, I don’t think they would be considered as legendary as they are.

“The moments in which shirts are worn and the players that wear them both contribute to the status of a shirt. That also speaks a little bit as to why retro shirts have become so popular.

“Legendary players from the 80s/90s seem cooler, perhaps because a lot of young people didn’t get to watch them play during their careers. Only getting to watch legends like [Gheorge] Hagi, [Marco] Van Basten, [Johan] Cruyff, [Michael] Laudrup, [Roberto] Baggio …through limited YouTube videos and highlight reels makes them appear all the more legendary. And that rubs off a bit on the status of the shirts that they wore.”

Robbie’s thoughts confirm the notion that retro jerseys have long been on the comeback trail.

Instagram is full of posts with throwbacks to iconic shirts of old – and to football’s traditions and magical teams. Boca Juniors, Fiorentina, Liverpool, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain, Barcelona, and more are just some of the clubs that feature heavily in posts dripping with charm, style, and those-were-the-days vibes.

After all, what football fan can scroll past a post of Diego Maradona in the pomp of his career wearing that special Mars-sponsored Napoli shirt without leaving an emphatic ‘like’?

Nostalgia is a big art of the apparent resurgence in popularity of retro replicas, but kit designer Robbie also believes retro shirts are popular because of something else, too “Retro shirts are baggier and made from materials that are almost closer to modern-day sweatshirts than football shirts. That plays well when it comes to fashion.”

Indeed, Icarus Football’s line of historical concept jerseys speaks to how sought-after retro-style kits are. “We really love working on our historical jersey range. We love history, and these jerseys are playful attempts at football shirts for bygone civilizations (e.g., Ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, The Republic of Venice, The Mongol Empire). There’s so much content to use as inspiration for these designs.”

New Amsterdam FC and Louisiana Krewe are two clubs Icarus FC have worked with in recent times, and they have also worked with clubs in the Ghana Premier League, among so many others. For several years, they have provided a nonconformist approach to fashioning beautiful jerseys shining with distinction. So, what about the future – what teams would Robby and his crew like to work with?

“At a top, top level, it would have to be a national team that’s open to something creative and experimental. National sides have so much imagery, history, and iconography that can be used for the purposes of a personal design. As a geography nerd, I’m extremely interested in working with national sides off the beaten path.

“I’d get just as much joy out of creating a design for Belize as for Brazil. Same thing goes for clubs. Give me TP Mazembe in the Congo, FC Noah in Armenia, and FC Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia (just to name a few) and I’d be a happy man.”

#2631. “We're still underrated in Germany” – Schlotterbeck backs Dortmund to keep title race open

Speaking after Borussia Dortmund's hard-fought 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich on Saturday, Nico Schlotterbeck said he believes the Black and Yellows are better than they are often given credit for in Germany.

The draw ensured Dortmund remain level on points with league leaders Bayern, trailing only on goal difference, and Schlotterbeck hopes a genuine title race will emerge as the season progresses.

“I think we're still underrated in Germany, partly because people keep saying that we don't play the best football. But we are good, and we know it. If we keep playing like this, I'm confident that we can keep things open for a very long time," Schlotterbeck told Kicker.

While acknowledging that Bayern are favourites to retain the title, the centre-back believes the Black and Yellows can challenge them if they continue to perform at their best.

“The only problem is that there are still more than 25 matchdays to go. We're in a good position and level on points with Bayern. You simply have to keep going and keep the title race open. We have a good team and can achieve something. But Bayern are the favourites, and we're the challengers," he said.

“However, if we perform over the coming weeks as we did today – or as we have done in certain halves of games this season – then we're in a good place and can certainly give ourselves a chance of keeping the title race open for a long time.”

While admitting that “not everything was perfect” in Saturday's draw against a side he himself has described as the best Bayern team of the last 10 or 15 years, Schlotterbeck believes Dortmund proved they can cause the Bavarians problems.

“We are good too. We showed that again today. The point was deserved. It's only one point, with plenty more still up for grabs in the title race, but it's already one more point than we managed to get against Bayern last season. We stuck with it, we're still level on points, and we put in a very solid performance – that's what I'm happiest about,” he remarked.

#2630. Victor Wembanyama on 60 Minutes: Spurs star explains why 'villain' label didn't bother him during NBA Finals

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Victor Wembanyama's 2025-26 season -- his third in the NBA -- affirmed his status as the league's next megastar. Wembanyama led the Spurs to the 2026 NBA Finals before they lost to the Knicks in five games, and he earned the first of what figures to be many Defensive Player of the Year awards and All-NBA honors.

Wembanyama has entered the 2026-27 season with sky-high expectations. The 7-foot-4 Frenchman is the favorite to win NBA MVP honors, and the Spurs are the favorites to win the 2027 championship.

For the better part of his first three years in the league, Wembanyama was a beloved figure, doing things no one else could do on the court to create jaw-dropping highlights that got passed around social media and group texts.

However, as the Spurs moved through the postseason, some of the love from fans started to get lost. There were moments that started to earn him a "dirty" label, including when Wembanyama clocked Naz Reid with an elbow in the second round of the playoffs against the Timberwolves. Wembanyama then irked Knicks players (and their fans) when he shoved New York star Jalen Brunson in the NBA Finals.

Once viewed as a conquering hero, Wembanyama became a villain, particularly in New York.

In a sit-down interview with 60 Minutes' Jon Wertheim that will air this Sunday night on CBS, Wembanyama was asked about that switch. He noted that he was unbothered by having a "villain" label because he was solely focused on what he was doing on the court.

60 MINUTES: Last year in the Finals you were portrayed-- as a villain. Correct me if I'm wrong, I didn't get the feeling that bothered you.

VICTOR WEMBANYAMA: No, it didn't because I'm not paying attention to this-- during the Finals. I don't think any player on either team really is.

While Wembanyama insists he ignored the chatter off the court, he doesn't seem to want that villain tag to last. Wembanyama added that last year's playoff run was a learning experience of toeing the line between being competitive and going to far -- which he noted he crossed on occasion.

60 MINUTES: I wondered if you didn't show, "Hey, this is part of my character too." Edgy Wemby, whatever it is. But you showed a new side of yourself.

VICTOR WEMBANYAMA: It showed my limits more than anything else. Going out there, you need to play basketball. You don't need to beat the s--- out of people. [laughs] If you wanna win, at least.

Wembanyama is one of the league's most openly introspective and reflective stars, even at just 23 years old. He seems to recognize that he allowed himself to get too caught up with the physicality of playoff basketball and seems determined to better understand how to play up to that line without crossing it in the manner he did at times in his first taste of the postseason.

TUNE IN: The full interview with 60 Minutes' Jon Wertheim and Wembanyama will air Sunday, Nov. 1 at 7:30 p.m. ET, after NFL football, on CBS and stream on Paramount+. In the preseason, 60 Minutes followed Wembanyama in his native France, where he runs an annual tournament combining basketball with another one of his passions: chess.

#2629. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2628. MLB rumors: Padres decline option on key rotation piece, Korean star to be posted

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only four days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Sunday's hot stove happenings.

San Diego's top two starters are now free agents. Two days after Michael King exercised an opt-out clause to become a free agent, the Padres declined their $14 million club option on Nick Pivetta, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Had the Padres picked up the option, Pivetta would have held an $18 million player option for 2028. That surely factored into the team's decision.

Pivetta, 34 in February, missed roughly five months with a flexor strain this past season. He returned late in the season and pitched reasonably well in six starts spanning September and the postseason. The San Diego Union-Tribune notes the Padres still have concerns about Pivetta's elbow, but could re-sign him to a new contract with a lower salary and/or no player option.

San Diego signed Pivetta to what amounted to a two-year, $23 million contact with two players options in February 2025. The flexor strain triggered an injury clause that converted the 2027 player option into a club option. We ranked Pivetta as the offseason's 43rd-best free agent.

As expected, the Orioles have declined their $20 million club option for center fielder Luis Robert Jr., reports ESPN. They will pay him a $2 million buyout, so it was functionally an $18 million decision. Robert suffered a hamstring injury and played only three games with the O's after being claimed off waivers from the Mets in late September.

Now 29, Robert again had multiple stints on the injured list this past season. He continued to punish lefties and play solid center field defense when healthy, but injuries have limited him to only 271 of 489 possible regular-season games from 2024-26. We did not rank Robert among our top 50 free agents, though he is an interesting upside play given his age.

The Hanwha Eagles of the Korea Baseball Organization will post star third baseman Si-Hwan Roh for MLB teams this offseason, reports Yonhap News Agency. Roh signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and $23 million), though as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the team once his MLB stint is over.

Roh, 26, has been one of the KBO's best players the last several years. He hit .283/.360/.505 with 29 home runs in 2026, and has averaged 35 home runs per 162 games since 2023. Roh is considered a reliable but unspectacular defender at third, plus he has first base experience as well. This free agent class is very thin at the hot corner. Roh should generate a good deal of interest.

KBO players get a 30-day negotiating window once officially posted. If Roh does not sign with an MLB team during the 30-day window, he will return to the Eagles. It's possible that Roh, a right-handed hitter, will eclipse his $23 million guarantee with the Eagles over just a handful of years with an MLB team.

The Astros have acquired Triple-A righty reliever Evan Reifert from the Rays for cash, reports the Tampa Bay Times. Houston is likely to add him to their 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. The Rays did not have the roster space to do that, so they traded for cash rather than lose him for nothing. Reifert, 27, has an excellent slider and used it to strike out 81 batters in 58 Triple-A innings in 2026. He should spend time in Houston's bullpen next season.

#2626. Mets legend Jerry Koosman dies at 83: Pitcher helped New York win 1969 World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Mets team Hall of Famer and two-time All-Star Jerry Koosman died Sunday morning in Osceola, Wisconsin, the team announced. He was 83. The Mets say Koosman battled multiple illnesses before his death.

"Kooz was one of the greatest pitchers in team history and a beloved member of the Mets family," Mets owners Alex and Steve Cohen said in a statement. "The 1969 Miracle Mets were filled with heroes, and the special southpaw from Appleton, Minnesota, was central to their success. He was a fierce competitor on the field, and respected teammate in the clubhouse. His legendary performance in the World Series helped the Mets secure their first Championship in team history. On behalf of the entire Mets organization, we extend our heartfelt condolences to Jerry's family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him."

The Mets discovered Koosman while he was pitching for the United States Army and signed him to a contract in August 1964. He made his MLB debut in April 1967 and moved into the rotation full-time the next season. Koosman threw 263 ⅔ innings with a 2.08 ERA as a rookie in 1968, which earned him an All-Star Game selection and MVP votes, and a second-place finish in the Rookie of the Year voting behind Hall of Famer Johnny Bench.

In 1969, Koosman was again an All-Star, throwing 241 innings with a 2.28 ERA. He was New York's No. 2 starter in the postseason between Hall of Famers Tom Seaver and Nolan Ryan. Koosman made two starts for the Miracle Mets in the World Series, including the Game 5 clincher against the Baltimore Orioles. He allowed three runs in the complete game win and recorded all but one possible out in his two World Series starts.

From 1968-76, Koosman was simply one of the best pitchers in the game, pitching to a 2.94 ERA and averaging 223 innings per season. The Mets traded him to the Minnesota Twins for Jesse Orosco in December 1978 and Koosman finished his career with stints for the Twins (1979-81), Chicago White Sox (1981-83), and Philadelphia Phillies (1984-85).

Koosman retired following the 1985 season with a 222-209 record and a 3.36 ERA that is 39th among AL/NL pitchers with at least 3,500 career innings. He ranks 35th all-time in strikeouts (2,556), 40th all-time in starts (527), 48th all-time in innings (3,839 ⅓), and 77th all-time in pitching WAR (57.0). Koosman went to two All-Star Games and finished second to Randy Jones in the 1976 Cy Young voting.

The Mets inducted Koosman into their Hall of Fame in 1989 and retired his No. 36 in 2021. His 140 wins are the most in franchise history among left-handers and third in team history overall, behind Seaver (198) and Dwight Gooden (157). Koosman is second in Mets history in innings (behind Seaver) and third in strikeouts (behind Seaver and Gooden).

Koosman fell off the Baseball Writers Association of America's Hall of Fame ballot in 1991, his first year of eligibility.

#2625. Pressing Impossible: Amorim Loses to Hürzeler – MH

von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren

Rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22. While Manchester United focused on creating a pressing system that was as difficult as possible to bypass, Brighton once again showcased their incredibly challenging vertical play. You can find the tactical analysis of the match here.

Manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession. Amorim initially placed particular emphasis on a pressing system that varied in height.

Meanwhile, Brighton began in a nominal 4-4-2 formation. In possession, Hürzeler’s trademark positional rotations, vertical runs, and decoy movements for effective vertical play were continuously on display. Accordingly, Brighton operated flexibly from a variety of shapes, such as 4-2-4, 3-1-4-2, 2-3-2-3, and more. This flexibility makes Brighton’s possession game almost impossible to define through formations alone.

Manchester United initially operated out of a 5-4-1 shape with varying defensive heights. This approach made it challenging for the opposition to play through, as different build-up phases required distinct patterns and connections. United’s central midfielders in the four-man line marked Brighton’s double pivot, Ayari and Baleba, man-to-man. The goal was to gain optimal control of Brighton’s central build-up play and apply immediate pressure whenever Brighton played through the middle.

However, Brighton controlled the game during the first 10 minutes. Their holding midfielders positioned themselves close to the backline, creating a large gap between Manchester United’s five-man defensive line and the four-man midfield. This space was then exploited with various runs. When facing high pressing, left-back Estupiñán moved asymmetrically into the left half-space behind United’s first pressing block. This movement utilized the moment when Amad stepped out to press one of Brighton’s center-backs after bypassing Zirkzee.

United failed to adjust their pressing to this build-up variation throughout the match. As a result, this same pattern played a key role in Brighton’s build-up to the goal that made it 1-3.

Against Manchester United’s mid-block, Brighton’s strikers, Welbeck and João Pedro, alternated their runs into the large space between the lines, targeting the gaps. This repeatedly allowed Brighton to bypass United’s first pressing line.

The 1-0 goal resulted from this setup, facilitated by a counter-movement. As striker Welbeck made a run into the space between the lines, he pulled his marker, De Ligt, a few steps out of the five-man backline. Simultaneously, winger Mitoma made a deep run into the space that opened up. De Ligt was caught in a dilemma between applying pressure and covering the depth. A long ball bypassed United’s entire pressing structure, leading to the goal.

Another reason for Brighton’s dominance in the first 10 minutes lay in their defensive work. United built up in a very positionally structured 3-2-4-1(/-5) shape. Brighton countered with a 4-4-2 in their high press and a 5-4-1 in their mid-block. With Minteh marking Diogo Dalot man-to-man on the flank, the two different defensive shapes emerged depending on Dalot’s positioning. Brighton’s two strikers also pressed United’s center-backs, Maguire and Yoro, on that side, applying intense pressure on the ball carriers on United’s left.

On the other side, winger Mitoma positioned himself centrally when De Ligt had possession, cutting off the passing lane to Amad, who was positioned in the half-space. If the ball was played to full-back Mazraoui, Mitoma shifted out from the center to press, creating a cover shadow into the center. This approach effectively prevented United from creating any significant attacking threat on that flank as well.

Around the 10th minute, the game shifted, and Brighton’s dominance began to fade. This was due to several adjustments made by United. To reduce the pressure on the ball carrier on the left side, the highly press-resistant Bruno Fernandes started to drop deeper, while the full-backs pushed higher. The resulting 3-3-4 shape was difficult for Brighton to press, as full-back Veltman, or the half-space defender in the five-man backline, was pulled out, and the space in behind could be exploited by either full-back Dalot or striker Zirkzee. This led to more possession phases for United and fewer pressing phases from Brighton.

Another adjustment United made came from their 5-4-1 mid-block. The half-space defenders, De Ligt and Yoro, became much more aggressive in stepping out from the five-man backline to defend against the strikers making runs into the large space between the lines. This prevented Brighton’s strikers from turning after bypassing the first pressing block. To defend long balls to Mitoma, Mazraoui prioritized covering the space behind the advancing De Ligt. As a result, Brighton struggled to exploit the space between the lines and couldn’t progress as effectively into depth from their own possession.

Additionally, Manchester United no longer pressed situationally from a 5-4-1 in a high press but instead switched to man-marking, with Zirkzee following the goalkeeper. This created much more pressure on the ball carriers for Brighton. Brighton also faced difficulties because the 5-4-1 system is much harder to break down than man-marking in a high press. This became evident in the sequence leading to the penalty goal. United suddenly switched to man-marking and forced the ball loss that preceded the penalty. United deservedly equalized.

After the 1-1, the game became more balanced. Brighton tried to break down the 5-4-1 mid-block, while United focused on their defensive game. When Manchester United switched to man-marking in the high press, Brighton continued to struggle and often lost possession. It is questionable why United didn’t press more boldly and high man-to-man during this phase to maintain better control of the game.

From Brighton’s perspective, a situational, more extreme overload at the moment of transition into high pressing—such as in the central space just behind the first pressing block—could have been a possible solution to challenge United’s man-marking, putting them in a dilemma between applying pressure and defending 1v1 on the wings.

In possession, Brighton’s players frequently adjusted their positioning with small movements, creating new passing lanes, changing passing angles, and occupying spaces that forced the opponent into pressing reactions. Below, I have outlined the main advantages of three of the most frequently used shapes by Brighton against United, as well as the necessary reactions from the opponent.

Another factor that makes Brighton’s vertical play difficult to defend is the continuous variety of space-creating or counter-movement runs into depth. These consistently create dilemmas and positional problems for the defenders. Below, I have graphically illustrated some selected runs used against United:

Despite Brighton’s possession game, Manchester United was able to prevent significant goal-scoring opportunities initially. From their 5-4-1 structure, the center-backs repeatedly defended aggressively, stepping out. Additionally, after bypassing the four-man midfield, it would drop back into position. This “recovery defense” made it difficult for Brighton to develop effective build-up play and exploit opened spaces. Furthermore, United’s players were well-prepared for potential through balls. In particular, the full-backs consistently intercepted balls played behind the defensive line.

Towards the end of the first half and into the second half, small (forced?) mistakes began to creep into United’s pressing. While the failure to step out with Ugarte in the man-marking high press in the 39th minute and the failure to step out with De Ligt in the space between the lines in the 38th minute went unpunished, the delayed step-out by Yoro led to Brighton’s deserved 1-2 at that point.

Especially in the second half, Brighton adapted to the man-marking high press by having center-backs step inside, breaking free from the cover shadow, when pressing the goalkeeper. This allowed them to find the open player in build-up, and Brighton lost possession less frequently.

Longer defensive phases in the mid-block for Manchester United followed. To break down this block, Brighton’s possession play became less positionally rigid. Much more frequently, certain zones were overloaded. In particular, the space between the lines and the half-spaces were repeatedly occupied by multiple players to create numerical superiority and apply pressure.

United, on the other hand, struggled to create any significant goal-scoring chances. The high press could have been more effective with a brief orientation from the player pressing the goalkeeper to position the inward-dropping center-back into a cover shadow. From the 5-4-1 mid-block, too few dangerous ball recoveries and transition situations were created.

Even from their own possession, Manchester United created too few goal-scoring opportunities. When Amorim’s team did get chances, it was typically through a ball played behind the wide players of the five-man backline. At the moment the press was triggered (when Brighton stepped out to the outer center-back), the forward half-space player dropped deep, and the winger made a run in behind. However, the lack of other ways to break the press led to too much predictability in United’s possession play.

As a result, the second half became more one-sided, with Brighton repeatedly pressing and trying to put United’s press under pressure. This ultimately succeeded, leading to a deserved 3-1 victory for Hürzeler’s team.

Amorim’s press, which was difficult to break down, was ultimately cracked by Hürzeler. It is questionable whether more frequent defensive pressing, alternating with situational man-marking high pressing, might have been a better approach against Brighton, in order to better tighten the space between the lines and the area behind the defense, making the game in depth more difficult. Despite a higher mid-block, Manchester United hardly created any dangerous transition situations. This is an area that needs improvement.

Hürzeler’s team, on the other hand, once again played highly attractive possession football. Frequent positional rotations, shifts in formations, overloads, and space-creating runs make Brighton’s possession game very enjoyable to watch. For the opponent, these constant shifts in zones over an extended period are incredibly difficult to defend. It is very likely that we will see more teams adopting similar principles in possession in the future.
