#2567. Yaxel Lendeborg continues to revive a Warriors team everyone left for dead

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Warriors fans are losing their collective mind over Yaxel Lendeborg, who continued to one-up himself on Sunday in leading Golden State to a win over the Clippers without Stephen Curry and Draymond Green. It was a completely outrageous performance: 37 points in 34 minutes on 68% shooting, including six 3-pointers.

The rookie added six assists. Threw in four boards and a steal for fun. What this guy has done over his first two NBA weeks is almost beyond comprehension. We're talking about the only rookie in NBA history other than Larry Bird to card at least 100 points, 40 rebounds and 20 assists through his first five games.

His sixth career game was his lone stinker. Luka Dončić gave him a proper hazing. But Lendeborg got right back on the horse on Sunday to become the fourth rookie in history to post 37 and five in a single game on 85% true shooting. Those 37 points are the most scored in a single game by a Warriors rookie since Curry had 42 in 2010, and Lendeborg now ranks as just the third Warriors rookie to average north of 20 PPG (22.3) over the first seven games of his career. The other two are Wilt Chamberlain and Rick Barry. Not bad company.

Yaxel Lendeborg scored 37 points to lead Golden State to victory, the most by a Warriors rookie in a game since Stephen Curry had 42 in 2010.Lendeborg is averaging 22.3 PPG this season, he's the 3rd player in Warriors history to average 20 PPG over his first 7 career games,… pic.twitter.com/T3RgsjFPB9

"That was a huge letdown last game," Lendeborg said of putting his foot in his mouth against the Lakers during his postgame interview. "I just try not to be a letdown again, honestly. I know I've got to keep my confidence no matter what goes on, good or bad game. And I just got to start playing with the joy that I played with the last six years of college and now here. So I'm just continuing to try to keep playing with a smile on my face, maybe throw a little dance move like Steph every once in a while. But I'm gonna just keep trying to find my joy."

Joy is an understatement. This dude's got Dub Nation flying. When I was growing up, there was a great song by Garth Brooks called "Unanswered Prayers," and I thought of it on Sunday as I watched Yaxel burying shot after shot from just about every spot and in every fashion possible, because I'll tell you this: a lot of Warriors fans are thanking the basketball gods that their pissed-off prayers to trade this summer's No. 11 pick fell on Dunleavy's deaf ears.

I mean, look at this guy, in his second week as a pro, chewing the Clippers up like a total 1A alpha.

Yaxel Lendeborg in win vs. Clippers:37 PTS6 AST4 REB13-19 FG6-11 3PTMost points in a game by a Warriors rookie since Stephen Curry in 2010.pic.twitter.com/rSIyjqIEmW

"He's playing this way and he really doesn't know the NBA game yet," Warriors coach Steve Kerr said after Sunday's game. "The game is still really fast for him, but he's so skilled and so talented that he's making all kinds of plays out there. It's remarkable the impact he's having on these games in the first couple weeks of the season."

Look at that reel. This is a rookie who played in just 11 high school games and had to start his career at a junior college taking over an NBA court like a coporate raider. Let's start with the one-on-one scoring, which he's doing in every manner possible: Bullying defenders in the paint, going by them off the dribble, pulling up from 3. Look at these isolation metrics from Tim Legler's All-NBA podcast:

This wasn't just a one-game thing, which, if you've actually been watching and have a functional pair of eyes, you already know. But the numbers are still startling. As further pointed out by the All-NBA pod, Lendeborg is currently the most efficient isolation scorer in the league at 1.52 points per direct play.

When he's not scoring one on one, Yaxel is running the floor like a Hummer or drawing two and dishing. With Curry out, he served as Golden State's point guard, which he noted afterward he's "always wanted to be." He calmed possessions like a veteran. Toggled between pick-and-roll handler and screener. Yaxel did al this while committing just two turnovers, which, during what has otherwise been an almost perfect first NBA impression, has registered as a lone hiccup.

But we have to get back to the shooting. Specifically, the pull-up shooting from range. It's one thing for a guy his size to be a spot-up threat, but this stuff off the dribble, in Kerr's words, "changes everything" in terms of Yaxel's potential.

"We knew he was a good shooter," Kerr said. "When he came in to work out, you could see the skill in terms of being able to put it on the floor and pull up and shoot, but I didn't expect what I saw tonight."

Frankly, you can remove the "tonight" from that answer. Anyone who says they expected anything close to what we've seen from Lendeborg at any point over these first seven games is a stone-cold liar. This dude is giving life to an old, decaying team that everyone left for dead this summer, and certainly after starting the year 0-3. The energy after four straight wins is undeniable. And now you have to wonder if the Warriors' front office has a mind to get aggressive on the trade market rather than waiting for their cap space to open this summer.

Because the simple truth is that Curry remains the best player in the world on any given night. Maybe that fact alone wasn't enough to justify putting the pedal down on this season before Yaxel emerged as a total beast, but now that he has, and with Jimmy Butler set to come back some time after the first of the year, this is a team that can really compete with another piece. They have the Draymond Green and Kristaps Porzingis contracts. They have the draft capital. They have Butler on an expiring deal if they want to go that route. The only question is, do they have the nerve?

#2564. Even Pellerud, a titan of women’s coaching, talks winning the Euros and World Cup

Even Pellerud is one of a select amount of head coaches who can say he won both a European Championship and a World Cup. He can also say he coached in a further two European finals and won an Olympic bronze medal. Not bad.

The 68-year-old is one of the most decorated coaches in the history of the women’s game at international level, with all his success coming with his home nation of Norway, while he also had a nine-year spell as Canada head coach where he pushed forward the development of the women’s game across the pond.

Across an hour-long interview from his home back in Norway, Pellerud reflects on what he constantly describes as a “lucky” career – not necessarily in terms of he didn’t work hard, but that he is privileged to have enjoyed so much success, especially when he discusses just how little he knew of the women’s game when he was asked by the Norwegian Football Federation to lead the women’s national team in the late 1980s.

After retiring from playing in 1986 and taking over as manager for the team he’d last played for, it was in 1989 that Pellerud’s coaching career took a new path, a path he would not look back from. “It was a strange incident really,” he chuckles. “I was asked to meet the federation. My name had started to grow a little bit, but I was kind of expecting it to be maybe one of the men’s youth teams.

“In the meeting, they offered me the job of the women’s team and that was a big shock for me. I think I had the right attitude for it, but I hadn’t actually seen one women’s game in my life, not even on TV.”

He adds, “They seemed to think I was the man for the job. I was ready to move on, so I was motivated and I wanted to be part of that environment, to grow something, that’s what really triggered me to do it. All I asked is that I have a contract for only two years, because I didn’t know how it would go.”

Two years would become seven, and an unprecedented period of success for Norway which saw Pellerud lead his nation to a European Championship in 1993, and after coming up short in the final of the inaugural World Cup in 1991, the grandest prize of all two years later in 1995, plus an Olympic bronze one year later in 1996, Pellerud’s final tournament of his first spell with Norway.

“To cut a long story short, I fell in love with the team,” he smiles. “We had a very strong team, a lot of success, I had a lot of fun. It was a great team to coach, such characters, such committed players. They were fit, well trained, it was just a fun team to work with and there was a lot of work to do, but it was a great job. It ended up being seven fantastic years.”

Pellerud inherited a side that included players who would go down in legend. Captain Heidi Støre, future Team GB head coach Hege Riise, one of Europe’s finest goalkeepers Bente Nordby and hotshot striker Linda Medalen, among many others.

Norway had won the first unofficial World Cup in 1988, but with a lack of footage, analysis or any of the things a modern-day coach would now have access to, a novice in the women’s game had no real understanding of where his squad of players was at heading into the World Cup, so how did he do it?

“That is a good question,” he exclaims. “Norwegian players in the league played in front of 50 spectators, in small venues, no media, they were playing games we won quite easily with the national team. It was only when we met Germany, Sweden or Denmark we were challenged.”

Pellerud, therefore, took his side to Winnipeg in Canada for a tournament against said hosts and the USA in 1990 to get a better understanding of what challenges he would face come the first World Cup in China, which was just a year down the line.

“That was the biggest eye-opener for me,” he recalls. “I was so happy we had that challenge. We beat Canada, but the USA just played us off the field, we had no chance. I think we lost 4-0 and it was a real shocker for me. I knew they were good because in 1988 the USA were the best team, even though Norway won, the coaches told me the USA were the best team. It was an eye-opener as to what to expect in China. We flew home and had some serious chats about what to do, how to bridge that gap in the space of a year.”

Pellerud admits going into the opening game, against the hosts, he had no real idea of what to expect, it was a whole other world to what his players had experienced back home, with the locals absorbing and engaging with the tournament on a level the women’s game hadn’t seen before.

“We went from these small games in Norway to 65,000 fans in China. Stands filled with people, we’d been in Europe and not seen this. My eyes were opened. Big buses, police escorts, people in the streets, it was so big you can lose yourself a bit. You don’t feel connected to the games or your team. The sound, the music, the opening ceremony, I will never forget the hours in the changing room after the opening game.”

Norway had lost 4-0 to hosts China and looked a world away from a side that would reach the final just a few weeks later. Pellerud and his side had been completely taken aback by what lay in front of them and had to act quick to ensure their tournament got back on track.

“We started well, we missed a penalty, but after that we didn’t have the ball, China totally outplayed us. That was my first World Cup game, you can imagine. We had to learn quickly how to raise a team that wasn’t used to losing, and here we are losing 4-0. They were rough days and for me, I learned a lot in that period.”

They bounced back to beat New Zealand 4-0 and Denmark 2-1, progressing past Italy in a dramatic and enthralling quarter-final, before disposing of neighbours Sweden in style with a 4-1 semi-final win.

The final didn’t go their way, a last-gasp Michelle Akers goal sealing the tournament for the USA, but Pellerud and his side had come so far from their 4-0 loss to the same opposition a year earlier, and had set the foundations for what was to come.

“We knew we had that level. We knew we had the players and we had the support from the federation,” he says. “The main thing for us was to create an environment where the players could be challenged enough in the league games. That was issue number one. We had to compensate for that by being super fit, super organised, we worked so much on defending. We had to introduce girls to training with the boys just to step them up a little bit. We had some really good years.”

“Good” is perhaps an understatement. Pellerud became European champion in 1993 when Birthe Hegstad’s late goal sealed a win in the final against Italy, before they headed to neighbouring Sweden in 1995 with renewed vigour ahead of the second World Cup. Riise was named player of the tournament and striker Ann Kristin Aarønes was the top scorer in the tournament with six goals, with Riise just behind on five. No other player for any country scored more than three.

Norway dominated from day one, winning all three group games without conceding and scoring an incredible 17 goals. They beat Nigeria 8-0, England 2-0 and Canada 7-0. A 3-1 win against Denmark in the quarter-finals was followed by the toughest test of all and a 1-0 win against defending champions USA.

Germany stood in their way of glory, but goals from Riise and Marianne Pettersen ensured it was Pellerud who came away as a world champion, and he admits he knew throughout the tournament his team would come out on top, and the feeling of being a world champion has only grown stronger in the subsequent 27 years.

“At the time, you live by the day, live by the training, live by the next game,” he says. “You don’t think so much about it, but I have to say in the years since it gets bigger and bigger for me. It was one of the tournaments where everything flies in your direction, everything we did was a success.

“We lost our captain in the semi-final against USA. Usually, we should be concerned, but we weren’t, we knew we were going to win. That is a very rare feeling for a coach. I’ve had that maybe twice in my life, that nobody was going to beat us.”

On the final itself, he recalls, “We pressed Germany super high. They got frustrated, we had full control, both games against them and USA was an extreme example of competitiveness, but not beauty. None of these games were beautiful. They were tough, a struggle, just don’t make mistakes, take your chances. But for the neutral, it was not fancy football. If Hege Riise and Linda Medalen and others played today, they would have been stars. The talent, the understanding of the game, the brilliant football minds. With today’s facilities, they would be stars.”

After a bronze medal one year later at the Atlanta Olympics which saw hosts USA win out in another tight semi-final, Pellerud stepped away and returned to the men’s game, but his affiliation with the women’s game was far from over. “The Olympics was another huge highlight in my life, but we weren’t quite as good, not quite as sharp, that was my feeling and I was right. I had many offers to coach men’s teams and had a desire in me to do that again.

“I’d got divorced and moved away from my home town, there were different things in my life which were both exciting and difficult. I was actually offered a lifetime contract with the federation.”

After a spell with Norwegian side Lillestrøm, Pellerud became the first Norwegian to coach a top division side in Denmark when he took over at Ikast FC. Three years since his last involvement in the women’s game, the opportunity soon arose to go back into it with another exciting new challenge.

“The General Secretary in Canada called me to discuss a contract to coach the women’s team. They had been very unsuccessful in 1991, 1995 and 1999 and wanted a European coach. It was a good fit in many ways. I’d remarried, we had two young twin daughters and we agreed on a mutual desire to see something of the world before the girls became too old. We went to Toronto, met the people, got a house, and like in Norway, two years became nine years!”

While now an experienced coach in the women’s game, Pellerud’s challenge almost outweighed that of him walking into the women’s game a decade previous with no knowledge of the sport, such was Canada’s position at the time.

After failing to qualify for the first World Cup, Canada went out at the group stage in both 1995 and 1999 and there was a lot of work to do for a country that was yet to embrace the sport of soccer.

“It’s almost impossible to think about,” says Pellerud of the challenge of taking on the Canada job. “It was not a soccer country then, there was no soccer on the news, no writing about it. The only information I had was that all my players after the 1999 World Cup were released from their contract. They said it was up to me if I wanted to bring anyone back.

“I didn’t complicate things, I ran around the country to see games that were set up as trials for the national team so I could see the best players in each province. I started to pick a team, had a camp in British Columbia and I used my contacts back in Europe to get us into the Algarve Cup in 2000.

Canada held their own with what was largely a brand-new side filled with young players, losing 4-0 to China, only 2-1 to Pellerud’s former employers and ending with a 2-1 win against Finland, followed by a 3-2 win against Denmark in the fifth-place match, a certain fresh-faced teenager by the name of Christine Sinclair scoring twice.

“Everything happened so fast, so fast. I had to take risks and I got a lot right, but some wrong. I had a couple of good leaders, then I had Christine Sinclair, that was the biggest thing. When I saw her in one of the setup games, I was quick to decide she would come to the Algarve with us. She was 16, but she was very special, so I built the team around these few players and played a very simple game. We pushed things, these players went from training twice a week to twice a day.

“We did ok, the federation was very helpful. We went to tournaments, we lost a lot, then we lost a little bit less, then we started to tie games and then we started to win. I promised the team we would beat the USA within a year, that was a bold statement, but we did. We beat them in the fall of 2000 in the USA, that was a very big moment for everyone.”

By the time the 2003 World Cup came around, Pellerud had been working on developing the Canada team for almost four years, but they still very much crossed the border to their tournament hosts as underdogs compared to the bigger nations. Pellerud though had a bit of “lucky timing” as he puts it, as FIFA introduced the first Under-20 World Cup a year earlier in 2002, to be held in Canada.

Given how young his senior squad was, many of them qualified for the tournament and indeed took part under the guidance of his assistant head coach, Ian Bridge. The squad would include six players who had gone to the senior World Cup a year later – Sasha Andrews, Carmelina Moscato, Brittany Timko, Kara Lang, Erin McLeod and Sinclair.

Canada reached the final, topping their group, before Sinclair scored an incredible five goals in a 6-1 win over England, another in a penalty shootout win against Brazil, before a narrow 1-0 loss to the USA in the final, but a core of Pellerud’s youngsters had gained valuable tournament experience.

“We had that advantage because these players came through together, they knew each other so well, had already played for the senior team and some got very good scholarships to go to the USA. That 2002 group was so talented, many went to 2003 and many others went to future tournaments. Some went on to play for Canada for years and years, so it was lucky for us with the timing.”

A year later, Pellerud led Canada out of a World Cup group for the first time and their dream journey continued with a 1-0 win against China in the quarter-finals. A 2-1 loss after two goals from Sweden in the final ten minutes denied Canada what would have been an incredible appearance in the World Cup final, but Pellerud had led them further than anyone could have imagined.

It meant expectations were high four years later when Pellerud took his team to his fourth World Cup, back in China where his journey had started 16 years earlier. The likes of Sinclair were now leaders of the team, while they’d been joined by other 2002 squad members such as Melanie Booth, Robyn Gayle, Andrea Neil, Tanya Dennis, Diana Matheson, Candace Chapman, Amy Walsh, Katie Thorlakson and Taryn Swiatek.

After defeat to Norway in their opening game, qualification was between them and final group opponents Australia. When Sinclair scored with five minutes to go it looked like Canada had narrowly avoided elimination, only for Cheryl Salisbury’s 92nd-minute goal to send Pellerud and his side home early.

“Oh yes … Australia,” he reflects. “We overachieved in 2003, we had some really good players, but at the same time we had major issues with funding moving forward. The federation didn’t care much, we basically lost all our funding, so we weren’t able to maintain that level. We trained a lot, maybe we trained too hard, maybe I asked too much of them. We had injuries so didn’t go to 2007 full strength or where we should be. It was disappointing.”

Pellerud went to another Olympics oneayear later but, after another narrow defeat to the USA, this time in extra-time, Pellerud decided that not only was it time to step away, but retire from coaching altogether. “It was always one goal. We could be competitive but we didn’t have the level to control games. We had to rely on Sinclair. The timing for a new coach was great because at this time these players were reaching their peaks. It was a solid foundation, so it was the right time for a new coach to come in with a new view.”

Pellerud had a deal in place to move into the shadows in a development role with MLS side Vancouver Whitecaps, but no less than a month after leaving the Canada role, another national team offer within the women’s game arrived in his inbox. It was from Trinidad and Tobago, very much still a developing nation in the women’s game and an even bigger challenge than Canada.

“I had a deal in Vancouver, then this thing with Trindad and Tobago came up and I was very surprised by it,” he recalls. “I didn’t know much about them, but it was a development opportunity to work with young players and that’s what I wanted.

“It was a fun experience. Different, not always easy, it was the opposite of easy, but I had good local staff. The general mentality was not really team orientated. There were social problems, getting a commitment was not easy and for me to try and get the best out of them was hard. We tightened discipline, we trained a lot and trained hard, but we started to increase the number of players and started to have a team that looked like a soccer team.”

After four years helping to develop the sport in the Caribbean, Pellerud was offered the chance to go back to where it all began – back to the Norway national team ahead of the 2013 Euros and the 2015 World Cup.

Norway was about to welcome an exciting group of bright young players including Ada Hegerberg, Caroline Graham Hansen, Maren Mjelde and Ingrid Engen. “There were some rumours Norway was looking for a technical director. I showed interest but they changed their mind, so that job no longer existed. Then someone said they were going to change their coach and would I be interested? I said ‘hell yes’, so I went for a meeting and the job was mine.”

It had been 17 years since Pellerud had last coached the national team and was welcomed by a completely new squad of players, but some of the brightest young players anywhere in Europe. “A lot had changed, but also a lot hadn’t changed,” he says. “Sometimes it felt like the world had stood still. I had the same number of support staff, even with Canada I had more. In 2013, nothing was really that different to 1995, that was surprising for me.

“I think perhaps they had rested too much on successes from the 1990s and not moved forward. I really liked the players though, it was a really talented group.”

With 18-year-old duo Hegerberg and Graham Hansen gaining plenty of attention and experienced heads such as Ingrid Hjelmseth, Solveig Gulbrandsen and captain Ingvild Stensland, expectations were high for the Euros in 2013.

Pellerud once again reached a major final, losing only 1-0, while missing two penalties, in a tightly contested final with Germany, but Pellerud was more circumspect in a different stage of his career and despite the defeat, talks of his return to Norway as one of the fondest times of his career.

“I had a fantastic time,” he smiles. “If you jump to the team I came back to, I was shocked by what I saw. The skill, the ball control, the agility, the love of the game and the intense play. That was another level, and there were many of them, not just the big names.

“I could not believe what Caroline could do with a ball, to me it was just unreal. What is going on here?! I had been so many years away and not really seen her. She was 17 when I came in, but what she did for me between 2013 and 2015 was unreal. She wasn’t a mature player then, but had pure talent, speed, agility, the solutions in tight situations. She was the closest I’d seen to the best men’s players.”

Pellerud’s last hurrah would come two years later at the 2015 World Cup, ironically held in Canada, and if not for a second-round defeat against England, his last game as a national team head coach could have come between the two nations he spent most of his coaching career with.

While Hegerberg’s emergence as one of the best young strikers in the world had plenty of eyes on Norway, Pellerud lost Hansen to injury before the tournament and despite a respectable draw against Germany in the groups, Norway bowed out after losing 2-1 to England despite taking a 1-0 lead.

“I was so happy and motivated going into 2015. The team was good, but I had some concerns because we had major problems with injuries, a lot of injuries. Caroline was not there at all, but we still did ok, we should have beaten England.”

He admits he had no idea going into the tournament that it would be his last, his departure was not pre-planned, but he quickly decided after that defeat that now past the age of 60, it was time to walk away. “After that game, I knew,” he reflects. “That was it for me. I went straight to the technical director. I said ‘you don’t even have to try and ask’, but he said take a holiday and call me again in 14 days. I said ‘you can call me, but it doesn’t matter’. He did call me and I said I didn’t have the motivation or the energy to raise a team again. It was actually a very easy decision for me and I went into a new position within the federation.”

Pellerud got the technical director role he’d applied for in the first place, a role he kept until 2018, and admits his days as a head coach are done, but he’s not against helping others via his own experiences.

More importantly, though, he ends our interview reflecting back on that “lucky” feeling, appreciating every day what he achieved across a 26-year career at international level, and the medals and memories he still cherishes. “I really wake up every morning and appreciate something I just regard as being there at the right time, I was the lucky one,” he says. “I’m healthy, I met amazing people, met amazing friends. I used to compete against them, but now I see them in hotels, airplanes, I was just so lucky.

“I cherish those years very much and it makes me happy now to be able to mentor young coaches. I enjoy travelling and meeting them and being an instructor on the UEFA Pro Licence courses. It helps me meet the next generation of coaches and to help them…with no ambition of taking their jobs.”

#2563. Luka Dončić explains his 'step forward' on defense after five-steal performance vs. Raptors

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Dončić currently leads the NBA in scoring by an astounding 8.1 points per game, as his 37.7 ppg average dwarfs Tyrese Maxey's 29.6 ppg in second place.

On Sunday night, Dončić increased that average with 45 points (along with 15 rebounds and six assists) in a 131-125 win over the Toronto Raptors, but after the game, much of the focus was on what Dončić did on the defensive end of the floor. Since he entered the league, no one has confused Dončić with an elite defender, but through six games this season, a leaner Luka has looked more engaged and improved on the defensive end for the Lakers.

Sunday night was his best statistical performance yet, as he produced five steals and drew three charges against the Raptors to give the Lakers eight extra possessions that became critical in a six-point win. That effort offered a proof point for Dončić of what he views as a genuine step forward he's taken on defense in his ninth season in the NBA.

"Obviously, I'm not the best defender in the NBA, but I think this year, I really took a step forward," Dončić said (via ESPN). "Obviously, people are going to talk what they want to talk [about] me. ... But I know, and my team knows, that I'm better this year."

Those three charges drawn now tie him for the most in the league this season, alongside Aaron Nesmith, Davion Mitchell, Draymond Green, Jalen Brunson and Keyonte George. He's averaging 1.8 steals per game, which is tied for 15th in the league, and while many will be quick to point out that charges and steals aren't necessarily a sign of great defense, they do point to Dončić's effort level being raised on that end of the floor.

For years, Dončić has been viewed as a one-way player. He is one of the elite offensive engines in the NBA, up in the tier with Nikola Jokić and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander for the title of best in the world. Defense has never been his calling card, and much of the frustration with Dončić's conditioning is due to a lack of effort on that end of the floor.

This year, Dončić seems to have bought into the importance of showing stronger effort on defense as he takes the reins as the Lakers' leader with the departure of LeBron James. Lakers coach J.J. Redick sees Dončić taking charges as him proving he's taking a step forward as a leader as much as anything.

"I think taking a charge in general is just a form of leadership, right? You're putting your body on the line for the team," Redick said. "... He's trying to win. You see the competitiveness come out so many times on the offensive end, but he's competitive on the defensive end, too."

Between Dončić and Austin Reaves, the Lakers have the potential to be one of the league's elite offensive units. The question coming into the season was whether they could do enough defensively to hold up with a roster that doesn't feature many high-end defenders outside of Walker Kessler.

Through seven games, the Lakers rank 20th in the NBA in defensive rating (113.9). While that's just a bit below league average, for a team with the second-best offensive rating in the league (119.9), it's enough to get the job done. The concern for the Lakers is whether Dončić and the rest will be able to maintain that effort level on defense as the season wears on.

It's easy to commit on the defensive end for a couple weeks coming out of camp, but it's much harder to be locked in 50 games into the season. The Lakers being 20th in the league in defense while touting Dončić's improvement on that end and an increased effort level suggests that if that commitment wanes from Dončić and others, their defense could crash closer to the league's worst units. That would negate the advantage they gain with an elite offense and bring them down a tier in terms of being a contender.

That will be worth monitoring as the season progresses, but for now Dončić and the Lakers are getting a proof point of what they can do when they're locked in defensively. Perhaps most importantly, Dončić is seeing that he can still be an elite offensive player while putting a bit more into his defense, which may make it easier for him to stay committed on the defensive side all year.

For the Lakers to be a threat in the West, the offense has to be elite but the defense needs to simply be serviceable. For now, they've figured out that formula, thanks in part to their star buying in and trying to lead by example with an increased focus on doing the right things defensively.

#2562. Grading every NBA lottery pick's first two weeks as impressive 2026 rookie class dazzles early

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

If there's one takeaway from the first two weeks of the 2026-27 NBA season (other than the fact that there are way too many injuries), it might be this: this rookie class has the potential to be the best in league history. Maybe that's an overreaction and a case of recency bias, but the stats and film don't lie.

This group of players was heralded as one of the best freshmen classes in college basketball history. Not only did those players meet expectations, but they also went beyond them. It's hard to see a collection of talent hitting college basketball again like that for a long time.

Wizards forward AJ Dybantsa was late to the party, but the No. 1 overall pick finally made his debut last week against the Cavaliers after missing the first four games due to an ankle injury. Dybantsa scored 19 points in his first game while being on a minutes restriction.

The biggest surprise in the NBA is the Memphis Grizzlies, the only team in the association that hasn't suffered a loss. Cameron Boozer, who has seemingly won at every place he's played — whether in high school, Team USA, Duke and now the NBA — remains the favorite to win NBA Rookie of the Year over Kings guard Darius Acuff Jr. and Bulls forward Caleb Wilson.

With the first two weeks of the season in the books, it's time to assess the play of every lottery pick from the 2026 NBA Draft by handing out some early grades. Let's dive in, starting with Dybantsa.

It took exactly 16 seconds to showcase one of Dybantsa's elite skills: drawing contact at the rim. In 35 games last season at BYU, Dybantsa attempted 296 free throws, which ranked No. 1 among all college players. That's going to be a huge part of his game throughout his career because of how good he is at getting into the lane and drawing fouls. He has already attempted nine free throws in his first two games. Dybantsa is still on a minutes restriction.

AJ Dybantsa looking comfortable in his second career game 😯17 PTS | 8 REB 🔥 pic.twitter.com/px5FjLar5t

Once that restriction gets lifted, he will play even more than the 57 minutes he played during the first two games combined. The Wizards have a chance to be a sleeper play-in team in a loaded Eastern Conference this season.

Peterson's role with Utah is still being established. Something that stood out to me was Jazz coach Will Hardy benching Peterson for the final stretch against the Spurs last week, even though the game went to overtime and the team was already without Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen. There were a handful of plays in the fourth quarter where Peterson didn't make the right read on the defensive end, but the decision to bench the young rookie and only play him 26 minutes might've cost Utah a chance to steal a game at home.

Despite Peterson still trying to find a clear-cut role, he ranks fifth in his rookie class among field goals attempted (78) this season. Peterson thrives on-ball but is also very capable off the ball. That's why I really liked him as a fit with the Jazz. Peterson is going to figure it out.

Boozer is the ultimate winner. Since high school, Boozer has a 155-17 record across games in high school, at Duke and in the NBA. It should come as no surprise that he's contributing to winning at the highest level. Boozer had his first career triple-double (18/12/12) and followed it up with a career-high 27 points against Sacramento. Even when Boozer isn't playing well, he can still impact winning with his passing.

Cameron Boozer career-high 27 vs Kings:27 PTS | 9 REB | 1 BLK | 8/14 FG | 77 TS% pic.twitter.com/vRuH59q21R

He is an elite processor of the game and it's only going to get better throughout his career. The one concern I do have about Boozer is the rim finishing. Per Synergy, he is shooting 42.4% at the rim. Aside from that, Boozer has been awesome. If the Grizzlies keep winning, Boozer should be the favorite to win Rookie of the Year.

The Bulls are off to a slow start, but Wilson is not. The way he can impact both ends of the floor remains one of his strengths. Wilson is also fearless and won't back down from anybody. Two of my favorite plays so far from the NBA season came in Bulls vs. Celtics games. On the defensive end, Wilson recovered while Jayson Tatum was driving middle and rejected him at the rim with his off hand. In a game against Boston days before, Wilson had the ball at the top of the key against Paul George, jab-stepped left and dunked it while taking contact.

look at this block by Caleb Wilson on Tatum omg pic.twitter.com/1vSkEUhaOU

He is averaging 3.2 stocks (steals and blocks) per game. Another note: He is taking 7.8 (!) 3-pointers per game after taking 27 total attempts at North Carolina last season. The efficiency (29.8%) isn't there yet, but if Wilson's shooting ticks up, it changes his entire ceiling.

Wagler has been playing in a sixth man role during the first two weeks. The Clippers are trying to bring him along slowly. I'll say this: It's time to start Wagler. He has looked very comfortable even dating back to his first minutes against Sacramento. Wagler is shooting better from 3 (31.3%) than 2 (24%), but I'm not super worried about the efficiency for him or any rookie guard on the list for one reason: Rookie guards are historically inefficient.

Again, it's understandable why the Clippers want to wait to start Wagler, but it's time to put him in the starting lineup and play him even more. Wagler has shown he's capable of taking on that responsibility while running the second unit.

Similar to Wagler, Brown is coming off the bench to begin his career. He has played over 25 minutes just once this season due to the team placing him on a minutes restriction. Brown also didn't play against Indiana last weekend due to back injury management. In the game (against Boston), where Brown played over 25 minutes, he was electric in the fourth quarter. Brown scored 13 of his 17 points in the final frame, including a corner 3-pointer to send the game to overtime. Brown made a rookie mistake in overtime, attempting a layup with less than five seconds remaining, with his team up by one and the shot clock off.

After that miss, Tatum knocked down a game-winner. Brown had NBA range during his time at Louisville, and that was on display against the Celtics. It's just a matter of time before Brooklyn lifts the minutes restriction and throws him into the starting lineup.

Acuff has become the most polarizing rookie to talk about. The Kings are bad. Like, potentially the worst team in the league. However, Acuff has been the bright spot. His shotmaking is second-to-none in his class. When Acuff is hot, he can score at will. Acuff joined exclusive company earlier this week when he finished with 34 points and 14 assists against the Pelicans. The only other teenager in NBA history to post at least 30 points and 12 assists in a game, per CBS Sports research? LeBron James.

DARIUS. ACUFF. JR.Shakes his defender and drills the 3!A game-high 21 points through two quarters for the @SacramentoKings' rookie 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/hA98OwsWvL

Acuff has the ultimate green light in Sacramento. It's going to stay that way throughout his rookie season. It feels more like a matter of when, not if, Acuff scores 45+ points in a game. It might even come before the calendar flips to 2027

Flemings' best game came last week against Miami, when he finished with 23 points, five assists, five rebounds and a block/steal. Flemings' role with the Hawks this season was always going to be off the bench, so it shouldn't come as a surprise that he has scored 27 points combined in the other six games he has played in.

Flemings doesn't have to score to make an impact on the game. He was heralded as one of the best two-way players in the class, which was on display in his last game against New Orlenos when he recorded four steals. Flemings uses his speed to his advantage to get to the rim, create his own shot and change the pace. Despite taking six field goal attempts per game, Flemings has been very efficient (47.6%).

Johnson has come off the bench in his first six games under his former college coach, Dusty May. Although his numbers don't necessarily pop, Johnson is going to be a very impactful player, especially on the defensive end of the floor. He's capable of guarding 1-5, which is super valuable when/if the Mavs decide to switch everything on defense.

Burries is coming off the bench for the Bucks, which somewhat surprises me. He was awesome in summer league and should be playing more than 16 minutes per game.

THIS DUNK FROM BRAYDEN BURRIES🤯14 points for the @Bucks rookie off the bench tonight! pic.twitter.com/H3Jk99cKn3

Burries did have one of the highlights of the season so far with a poster dunk over Tristan Enaruna. That game was also the highest-scoring (14 points) game of his so far.

Lendeborg is one of the most entertaining players to watch. You either love him or hate him, but you're still going to watch. It should come as no surprise that it took him exactly one game to talk trash to the opponent, which nearly backfired when Luka Dončić went on to drop 37 points less than 10 days after the season opener.

The highs of Lendeborg's rookie season so far have been fantastic. Even though he had his worst statistical game against the Lakers, he finished with at least 25 points in three consecutive games, including a 31-point, 12-rebound outburst against the Nuggets. Yes, Lendeborg may be the oldest rookie from the first round of the draft, but it's clear to see why the Warriors drafted him. He is already Golden State's second-best player behind Steph Curry, which shouldn't even be that hot of a take. Lendeborg was awesome in a win over the Clippers and scored a career-high 37 points. He should be the co-favorite with Boozer for ROTY.

It's going to be sink-or-swim for Mara, with Chet Holmgren becoming the latest Thunder player to suffer an injury that will sideline him for multiple weeks. Mara logged 28 minutes against the Rockets and finished with seven points, nine rebounds and four blocks. Mara was one of the most efficient scorers at the rim and also one of the top shot blockers in college basketball because of his long 7-foot-3 frame. Mara has a chance to contribute in a larger role with Holmgren out. He's going to be just fine.

Ament was a DNP-CD in Ament's first two games before making his first appearance against the 76ers. Ament has skill and potential but is one of the rawest players drafted in the lottery. The Bucks are bringing him on slowly, which should do wonders for his development. He shot under 40% from the field last season at Tennessee but has been solid in that department (45.8% from the field, 44.4% from 3) in four games. The sample size isn't large enough to give a definitive grade, but Ament has shown signs of improvement since his college days. He has also been solid on the defensive end of the floor.

Steinbach has played in just two games this season, both of which came in garbage time. He played 12 minutes in a 121-81 loss to the Hawks and two minutes against the Wizards last week. Coming into the season, I expected Steinbach to play a larger role. That could still happen later in the season, but the sample size so far isn't large enough to hand out a letter grade.

#2561. Russell Westbrook number retirement: OKC Thunder to hang No. 0 from the rafters in February

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Oklahoma City Thunder will put Russell Westbrook's No. 0 into the rafters at the Paycom Center on Feb. 7, 2027, when they host the New York Knicks, the team announced on Monday.

0 Forever 💙02.07.27 pic.twitter.com/pTqRnespU2

Westbrook retired this offseason after an 18-year career that saw him make nine All-Star teams, nine All-NBA teams and win the 2016-17 MVP award. All but one of those All-Star and All-NBA seasons came as a member of the Thunder; he averaged 23.0 points, 8.4 assists, 7.0 rebounds and 1.8 steals per game across 821 appearances in an Oklahoma City uniform.

"Many players make an impact but only great players leave a legacy. Russell Westbrook's legacy was built both on the court and in the community," general manager Sam Presti said in a statement. "His mindset was relentless, his commitment deep. For all those reasons, Oklahomans consider him one of their own and his number will be raised to the rafters, in Oklahoma City forever."

The Thunder traded Westbrook to the Houston Rockets before the 2019-20 season, but he struggled to stick with a team for long. While he remained productive, he bounced from Houston to Washington to Los Angeles (both the Lakers and Clippers) to Denver to Sacramento before calling it a career, never lasting two full seasons in the same place.

After a rash of injuries in Oklahoma City and with Westbrook's retirement still fresh, some wondered if the Thunder might consider calling in Westbrook for reinforcements on the roster. When asked about that possibility following Jalen Williams' season-ending injury and Cason Wallace's shoulder surgery, Presti insisted he hadn't considered any roster moves at that time.

"I haven't thought about anything relative to the roster spot," Presti said during a press conference last week. "I understand the question, but all I'm really focused on right now is players, getting them the right support, and then helping everybody with our group realize that, you know, we have a tremendous challenge in front of us."

From a basketball perspective, the fit between Westbrook and this current Thunder roster would've perhaps been a bit clunky, but many wondered if OKC still might pursue it as a fitting, emotional send-off for the franchise's favorite son. With the announcement of his jersey retirement, that puts to rest any speculation he'll end his retirement to return to play for the Thunder. Still, he'll get to return to the only team he ever called home long-term -- and the only fan base that ever truly embraced him.

"Let Westbrook be Westbrook" was a favorite saying during his prime years in Oklahoma City, and it's the only place he ever was able to do just that. After Kevin Durant left for the Warriors, Westbrook became the avatar of loyalty in OKC, and the Thunder faithful latched onto their star guard even more after feeling betrayed by Durant.

While it didn't yield the championship Westbrook and Thunder fans hoped for during his tenure, he is the most beloved figure in franchise history for what he did to establish NBA basketball in Oklahoma City and give back to the community. On Feb. 7, he'll get a chance to receive a long-awaited warm welcome back to his adopted home and see the No. 0 get raised to the rafters.

#2560. Steelers' Jaylen Warren is 'on fire': Why the breakout running back keeps getting better

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

PITTSBURGH -- On a team that includes several future Hall of Fame players, Jaylen Warren was the talk of the Steelers' locker room following a 27-6 trouncing of the Browns that gave Pittsburgh the outright lead in the AFC North division.

Warren, who turned 28 on Sunday, celebrated the occasion by rushing for 143 yards (tying his career-high) and a touchdown on 17 carries. It was the second consecutive 100-yard game and the fourth 100-yard game of the season for Warren, a former undrafted rookie who in the midst of a career year.

"Jaylen is on fire," coach Mike McCarthy said afterward. "You can't get him the ball enough."

“Jaylen is on fire. You can’t get him the ball enough.” #Steelers coach Mike McCarthy on Jaylen Warren. pic.twitter.com/b3e2gtBCbQ

Why is Warren's level of success enhanced in Year 5? It starts with his featured role. On Sunday, Pittsburgh's offensive line bullied Cleveland's defensive front to the tune of 200 yards and three touchdowns on 33 carries. It was a unit that was clearly motivated to respond to Cleveland pass rusher Jared Verse's recent comments with their play on the field.

Most everyone who watched Sunday's game saw Steelers guard Mason McCormick's body slam of Verse in the first half. But just as telling was McCormick and center Zach Frazier sprinting to the other side of the field at the end of the first quarter. While his teammates were running, fellow Steelers lineman Brock Hoffman made a "feed me" reference to the Steelers' sideline, a subtle request to McCarthy to continue running the ball.

Pittsburgh's defense has also helped Warren and the offense. The Steelers' defense, which hasn't allowed a touchdown in seven quarters, has enjoyed more time on the bench while watching Warren do his thing.

"He's a bowling ball with teeth, man," said Steelers linebacker T.J. Watt, who had two of Pittsburgh's eight sacks of Deshaun Watson. "You can't get him down. Jaylen is just funny, man. He's the guy that's out there in December when we're practicing and it's like 12 degrees, he's in a T-shirt and shorts. You're like, 'What the heck?' That's just who he is. He's a hard tackle. He's a great locker room guy. Very selfless. But man, he loves football and you can see it in the way that he plays."

Cam Heyward, the longest-tenured Steelers player, gave Warren the ultimate compliment.

"I've been blessed to play with a lot of great running backs. Jaylen is not short of that," he said. "He's every bit as advertised. Having Rico [Dowdle] as well, they do a great job of being a 1-2 punch. When they're able to sustain drives, it means we're on the sideline and we can put our feet up."

Speaking of sustaining drives, that's what Warren did on his 51-yard run that came on a third-and-13 play. The play helped give the Steelers their first double-digit lead of the day.

"To be able to call a trap on third [and long] and get a first down is pretty wild," Rodgers said. "Didn't expect that. Can't remember the last time that happened when I was out there."

Jaylen Warren just went 51 yards on 3rd and 13 😳CLEvsPIT on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/YD1Naon9lN

The biggest reason for Warren's emergence, though, is the man himself, although Warren's humility would never allow him to say that himself. Warren has only gotten better during his time with the Steelers.

After a somewhat disappointing 2024 season, Warren told CBS Sports that he planned to spend more time getting treatment at the facility. That change has clearly helped. Warren ultimately ran for a career-high 958 yards in 2025 and is currently on pace to have the most prolific rushing season by a Steelers running back since Le'Veon Bell.

"It's definitely paying off," Warren said on Sunday when asked about his extra time at the recovery table.

“I’d say it’s definitely paying off.”#Steelers Jaylen Warren on some of the changes that have led to his success. pic.twitter.com/J6JV2Gm0s5

Lastly, Warren's intangibles are another reason for his success. His team-first attitude has made him a locker room favorite. His teammates want him to succeed, which is evident every time he makes a big play and whenever his teammates are asked about him.

“Love having him on our team. He’s a fantastic teammate, and he’s making a lot of plays.” #Steelers Aaron Rodgers on Jaylen Warren. pic.twitter.com/RtCUght8GR

For Warren, it's about being the best player he can be so he can help the Steelers achieve their Super Bowl goals. That mindset helped him make the Steelers' roster as an undrafted rookie, and it's serving as the main catalyst for his breakout season.

#2559. Why Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg was benched after being 'peer pressured' into chasing 40 against Clippers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Golden State Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg has been a revelation to open his NBA career. Through his first seven games, he's putting up historic numbers, and he somehow keeps one-upping himself. On Sunday, he played his best game yet: 37 points on 85% true shooting. He made six of his 11 3-pointers and added six assists. He was outrageously good, as he has been all season, save for the Lakers game last Friday in which he was properly hazed by Luka Dončić.

Other than that, it's been nothing but buckets for Lendeborg, who, given how easily all this has seemingly come for him, perhaps got a little ahead of himself by chasing the 40-point round number on Sunday with a couple of, shall we say, questionable shots at the end.

Steve Kerr saw it, and with 2:14 to play, he benched his rookie as the Clippers were starting to make a desperate run, cutting a 21-point Warriors lead to eight over a two-minute span during which Lendeborg missed three 3-pointers, two of which were total chuck jobs.

"He would've had 40 if we had just kept playing [normally]," Kerr said after the game. "The NBA game these days can change like that. We all know that. Almost every night, there's a 25-point lead that is overcome.

"The game changed when all the guys on the bench were yelling at Yax to get 40. He launched three kind of bad shots. A lesson is, if you just keep playing, then you stay in rhythm, you stay in flow, the ball moves, and then the game becomes much easier. I think that's the lesson for him and for our team.

"But everybody loves Yax. Everybody wanted him to get 40. They were urging him to shoot from the bench, and It got us out of rhythm a little bit."

As soon as Lendeborg went to the bench and the Warriors got back to business, De'Antony Melton, who was a stud all night, buried back-to-back 3s to put the game back on ice. It was a great night for the Warriors, who've won four straight after opening 0-3, and for Lendeborg, who continues to be a total open book who is more than willing to admit to his mistakes and vow not to repeat them, as he did after the Lakers debacle when he took full accountability for "wetting the bed."

Yaxel Lendeborg was chasing 40 points late and it let the Clippers back into it briefly. He said he fell into peer pressure. It was his lesson of the night: "I've never been a stat chaser...I'm a guy that loves ethical hoops."Full Yaxel + Steve Kerr soundbite pic.twitter.com/5Lyo3CVXMb

"I've never been a stat chaser in my life," Yaxel said after he was benched on Sunday. "So, I mean, just falling into peer pressure like I did just now was pretty much bad on my part. Especially just, I'm a guy that loves, like, ethical hoops. I'm a guy that loves efficient basketball, and I didn't do that for the last two to three minutes. So, it's kind of, like, bad on my part. Next time I definitely won't do that again. If it comes to me, it does. If I don't get it, then I wasn't meant to get it that day. So, I'm gonna be way better next time."

Lendeborg elaborated on the peer pressure aspect of the chase, which, frankly, anyone can understand. You're a rookie and you're going off and your teammates are all cheering you on to keep shooting. The game, you think, is in the bag. Any player in that situation would've let a few more shots go.

"De'Anthony Melton went up to me and said, 'Hey, man you need to get 40. You're three points away,'" Lendeborg said. "And I'm like, 'Nah, It's all good.' He just peer pressured me into doing it. ... He said he's gonna give me the ball, and he literally was holding it just to give me the ball. I'm like, all right, fine, I'll shoot it,' and I missed. I tried to tell him 'no, no, no,' and now Will [Richards] came over [to me saying], 'you gotta do it, you gotta do it.'

"So everybody was just egging me on and I kind of just fell into it. But I know next time I'm just going to play in the flow of the game, because [the Clippers] came down and made like four threes in a row and we almost lost the game because of that. So next time I'm never doing that again."

#2558. Frankfurt’s pressing adjustments secure victory over Galatasaray – MH

von Next Generation am 22.09.2025 in den Kategorien Champions League mit 1 Kommentar

Eintracht Frankfurt won their opening Champions League matchday with a 5-1 victory over Galatasaray Istanbul. After about ten minutes, Frankfurt were trailing 0-1, but thanks in part to adjusted pressing, they were able to turn the game around. What follows is an aspect analysis of Frankfurt’s attacking press against the Istanbul side’s build-up play.

Frankfurt started, as usual, in a nominal 4-2-3-1. Ahead of the two midfielders Chaibi and Larsson, Uzun operated in the No. 10 role. On the left flank, winger Knauff played in front of left-back Brown. When dropping into a deeper defensive press, this structure shifted into a 4-4-2, with Burkardt and either Uzun or Knauff forming the first pressing line. In the transition to the attacking press, they shifted man-oriented as usual.

Galatasaray also began in a nominal 4-2-3-1. In possession, their structure changed depending on the depth of their build-up, forming something like a 3-2-5 or 4-2-4 through the positioning of the full-backs. Width on the right side was provided by winger Sané, and on the left by full-back Elmalı. Left winger Akgün frequently moved inside, acting as a kind of “free player.” Meanwhile, right-back Sallai tucked in slightly in higher possession phases to help form a back three in the build-up.

Galatasaray’s build-up was characterized by frequent rotations. Their basic reference point was the previously described 3-2-5. From this shape, they consistently sought positional interchanges in order to manipulate the opponent’s man-marking in the pressing phase. On the left side, Elmalı, who provided width, was able to vary his height. In deeper build-up phases, he often dropped further back, while he also regularly positioned himself on the last line. Winger Akgün was tasked with creating central overloads and repeatedly moved inside, at times even drifting over to the right side. In response to the full-back pushing high, the left holding midfielder, Lemina, rotated into the left-back position. Striker Yılmaz, in turn, shifted into the left half-space when the full-back stayed deeper and the winger dropped centrally.

Galatasaray’s left-sided rotations force Frankfurt’s pressing players into constant reorientation.

The purpose of these rotations was to manipulate man-marking and tie down specific Frankfurt players. Because winger Akgün frequently dropped into central areas, the two centre-backs, Koch and Theate, were occupied. Akgün positioned himself in front of striker Yılmaz in order to stretch the last line and create 1v1 opportunities. This produced a variety of different build-up structures, which required Frankfurt to constantly reorient themselves. For example, if Elmalı pushed high, he had to be tracked by Collins, and Galatasaray’s four attacking players tied down Frankfurt’s entire back line. This significantly complicated Frankfurt’s transition into man-marking, as the positioning of the forwards forced centre-back Theate to cover long distances during handovers.

Since all players in the back line are occupied, defensive handovers become more difficult.

Frankfurt’s plan, as in previous matches, was to shift into man-marking from a +1 overload through the handover of the opponents’ centre-backs and full-backs. The advantage of this approach is that spaces on and behind the last line can initially be secured, while the risk of a long ball leading to a 1v1 situation is minimized by having an additional covering player.

At the same time, after steering the opponent’s attack, the transition into man-marking could be executed to apply maximum pressure on the ball carrier. Depending on the opponent’s structure and build-up sequences, Frankfurt adapted their pressing schemes. For instance, they could vary the distance to their opponents during the pressing jump: larger distances allowed for greater security in coverage, while smaller distances created more immediate pressure.

Galatasaray tried to make these handover moments as difficult as possible for Frankfurt by forcing the distances at the moment of transition into man-marking to become as large as possible. The aforementioned rotations, for example, forced Theate into long runs to pick up winger Sané, so that Brown could then jump out to the still unmarked and deeper-positioned right-back of Galatasaray.

Because of Galatasaray’s attackers’ positioning, Theate and Brown are forced into long pressing runs. On top of that, Theate finds himself caught between two opponents due to the rotations.

Galatasaray also tried to open up the center through certain rotations, aiming to draw Frankfurt’s midfielders out of central areas. Frankfurt tracked man-to-man with Larsson on half-space player Gündogan and Uzun on the deeper right-sided pivot Torreira. Depending on the side of build-up, Chaibi was prepared to jump onto the more advanced pivot, Lemina. Because Lemina often rotated into the full-back position, Doan frequently picked him up, leaving Chaibi or Collins (depending on the movements of Akgün and Elmalı) unexpectedly without a direct opponent. At the same time, Gündogan and Torreira sometimes rotated in opposite directions, which created difficulties for Frankfurt in terms of handovers in central areas.

Because Frankfurt found it increasingly difficult to press Galatasaray’s build-up through their usual handover approach, from around the 15th minute they opted for tighter marking distances to transition more quickly into full man-marking. Brown pushed up directly, Theate went straight onto Sané, while Collins and Koch marked the two remaining forwards. This created a 3v3 situation on the last line. Although this increased the pressure on Galatasaray and led to more turnovers in their build-up, it also raised the risk against long balls due to isolated 1v1s. Time and again, Galatasaray managed to exploit this by sending strong dribblers like Sané into such spacious 1v1 situations. Even so, the tighter marking distances resulted in a much more balanced game with more frequent ball recoveries.

In the 30th minute, Frankfurt used a longer stoppage to make more significant pressing adjustments. Winger Knauff no longer pressed Galatasaray’s right centre-back but instead oriented himself toward full-back Sallai. This allowed Brown to stay on Sané, and Theate no longer had to make long runs out wide to cover him. At the same time, it was no longer problematic if all four defenders were tied up, as they no longer needed to jump out of the back line. The free centre-back was now primarily pressed by Uzun, who used his cover shadow to block passing lanes into pivot Torreira. Galatasaray’s build-up on the right side could then be pressed man-to-man through ball-oriented shifting. To this end, Chaibi stepped onto Uzun’s original opponent, Torreira, and the far-side Doan also moved into the ball-near center.

Frankfurt’s pressing adjustments: With no need to shift across the last line anymore, Frankfurt gains situationally much better access with less risk. These changes spark the turnaround in the match.

The pressing adjustments led to significantly better situational access and, at the same time, to much stronger defensive security. Frankfurt were able to use the resulting ball recoveries to establish longer possession phases, which gave them a more dominant style of play. One such spell of possession resulted in the 2-1 lead shortly before halftime. Immediately afterwards, a ball recovery from the adjusted attacking press led to a free kick, which in turn produced the 3-1 at the break.

In the opening 30 minutes, Galatasaray were able to cause Frankfurt problems, thanks in part to a very elusive build-up play that challenged Frankfurt’s typical pressing approach with its reliance on handover moments. Frankfurt’s adjustments, however, proved perfectly suited to applying pressure more easily while also improving defensive cover. The short interruption of play came at just the right time for Toppmöller and his coaching staff to implement the necessary measures. As a result, the pressing changes were decisive for Frankfurt’s eventual 5-1 victory and a successful start to their Champions League campaign.

#2554. Cowboys should consider trading George Pickens: 5 logical NFL deadline destinations

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ARLINGTON, Texas -- Shortly after Chad Ryland's game-winning field goal went through the uprights to seal a 33-30 comeback, Dallas Cowboys wide receiver George Pickens flew down the hallway and into the locker room by himself. No other teammate, coach, or staff member moved faster to get into the locker room and out of AT&T Stadium after Dallas made ugly history with its blown 14-point lead.

Pickens first one to the lockers, jogged down the tunnel before most media could even set up @1053thefan pic.twitter.com/RVab4T1c5M

Pickens' lack of targets was glaring. CeeDee Lamb led the way with 11 targets on Sunday while tight end Brevyn Spann-Ford was second with five targets. Pickens caught two passes for 48 yards. Four targets in a game simply isn't enough.

Pickens hasn't been bad this season: his 533 yards receiving rank as the 15th most in the NFL in 2026, just behind Trey McBride and just in front of Garrett Wilson (527) and Ja'Marr Chase (492). He is still on pace to exceed 1,100 receiving yards, but it regularly feels like the Cowboys are leaving production out on the field. Since Schottenheimer blamed Pickens' lack of vigor for run blocking for the team's struggling offense in a loss to the Green Bay Packers, he has 10 targets across the last two games.

"If I had the answer, we'd get him involved. I'm not trying to be rude or whatever it is, but he made some plays. Anytime the ball went his way, he came up with them. He had the one, unfortunately came back for a holding," quarterback Dak Prescott said. ... "I'm not sure about even how many targets he had. As I told y'all before, I go through the reads. [I] try to throw it to the open guy and stay consistent and true to that. And so, I've got to go back and look at the film and see if I missed him, see if we could have went to him more, see if we could have went to CeeDee more. I feel like it was a game that CeeDee didn't have as many catches as per usual, but we still had a chance to win and should have won it."

With the NFL trade deadline coming up in eight days on Nov. 10 and the Cowboys off to a 3-5 start and appearing to be going nowhere, it would make sense for Dallas to field trade calls for Pickens. He is playing out the franchise tag, and he will command near-top-of-the-market value on his second multi-year NFL contract. Dallas will also have to deal with balancing cornerback Joey Porter Jr.'s contract situation, since he, too, is set to be a free agent after the season.

After trading away draft capital to get Porter Jr. and Quinnen Williams, Dallas could use some additional ammunition in its 2027 NFL Draft war chest. So who could be blowing up owner/general manager Jerry Jones' phone for Pickens if word leaks out that they will listen to trade calls for their 25-year-old Pro Bowl wideout? Here is a look at five potential landing spots.

Jerry Jones has shown he doesn't care about sending a young star player to a non-divisional rival: he traded Micah Parsons to the Green Bay Packers. The pairing of the 49ers and Pickens makes too much sense.

San Francisco is the NFC's top seed through the first eight weeks of the season, and they have $34.98 million in cap space, the third most in the entire league, per OverTheCap.com. There are no financial barriers to this deal.

Plus, they have a glaring need for Pickens given all their wide receiver injuries. Both Mike Evans (ribs, Achilles) and Deebo Samuel (hamstring) were ruled out of their last game played in Week 7. Three wide receivers are on their injured reserve list.

Lastly, the 49ers are all in for 2026 because of their aging core. Christian McCaffrey is 30, Evans is 33, Samuel is 30, George Kittle is 33, Kyle Juszcyk is 35, Trent Williams is 38 and DeForest Buckner is 32. Both Fred Warner and Nick Bosa are healthy right now, but they're both 29 with extensive injury histories.

The Chiefs failed to score a game-winning touchdown after having a second-and-goal at the one with 15 seconds left, and Kansas City was outscored 15-0 in the fourth quarter of their narrow 28-24 road loss against the Denver Broncos on Sunday. You know who could have made a significant difference for quarterback Patrick Mahomes in the fourth quarter in Week 8? The 6-foot-3, 200-pound Pickens.

Kenneth Walker III is starting to lose a little steam after being heavily relied upon to carry the Chiefs' offense on his back. After averaging 133 rushing yards per game and 6.3 yards per carry with six rushing touchdowns in Kansas City's first five games of the season, Walker III is now averaging 52.5 rushing yards per game and 3.0 yards per carry without a touchdown in the last two games.

That's because the Chiefs' passing game requires Travis Kelce to be their No. 1 target, something that isn't a sustainable formula over the course of an 18-week season and beyond. Also, it would be incredibly foolish to waste the rest of Mahomes' glory years. The three-time Super Bowl MVP quarterback is 31, but he hasn't been the same high-flying passer that he was with a true No. 1 wide receiver like Tyreek Hill. Without Hill since 2022, Mahomes' production has taken a notable dip.

* Ranks among 37 qualified quarterbacks since 2022

The Buffalo Bills are the AFC's No. 1 seed through the first eight weeks, and they are always in win-now mode with Josh Allen. Yes, the Bills traded for DJ Moore, but he is probably best as Buffalo's No. 2 receiver on a Super Bowl team. He missed Buffalo's last two games with a shoulder injury prior to returning in Week 8, and he hyperextended his knee in the Bills' 36-10 beatdown of the Lamar Jackson-less Ravens.

Allen hasn't had a true WR1 since the 2024 Stefon Diggs trade. Pickens could help him become the league's most efficient passer. That would probably be enough for the Bills to perhaps win their first Super Bowl in franchise history.

The Las Vegas Raiders trading for Pickens would be a case of taking care of the now and the later. The Kirk Cousins-led Raiders are 4-4 and just one game out of the AFC's No. 7 seed. Giving Cousins, whose 19 passing touchdowns rank as the second most in the NFL, Pickens to pair with Brock Bowers could really make Klint Kubiak's offense pop.

Among the players officially listed as wide receivers on the Raiders' roster, Tre Tucker, a 2023 third-round pick, is the best they have. He could also help accelerate Fernando Mendoza's long-term development. Pickens is just two years older than the 23-year-old Mendoza, so the quarterback could spend the bulk of his career with a high-caliber wide receiver in addition to the 23-year-old Bowers at tight end.

Perhaps living in Las Vegas would dull the novelty of going out on The Strip that Pickens and Lamb experienced when they visited for "Monday Night Football" last season.

Despite being 6-1 and the No. 2 seed in the NFC, the Minnesota Vikings have the sixth-lowest scoring offense (20.0 points per game) in the entire NFL. Their lack of rhythm in the passing game is a major reason for that, as their Kyler Murray-quarterbacked passing attack is averaging the second-fewest passing yards per game (165.6) in the entire NFL.

Yes, Minnesota has 2022 NFL Offensive Player of the Year Justin Jefferson and former first-round pick Jordan Addison at wide receiver, but its offense could clearly use another weapon to help Murray find his groove as a Viking. They have been rumored to be in pursuit of Jonathan Taylor, but perhaps Pickens could also help fix the issues on the offensive side of the ball.
